statement: Pew’s November 2014 surveys found smartphone ownership among 64% of US adults, against 35% in 2011; 7% of adults had both no home broadband and few alternative ways to get online.

sources.supports: Ownership history and conjunctive definition.

counterevidence: A broader measure gives 19% experiencing at least one constraint, and should not be called the same dependent group.
inference_limits: Late-2014 observations published in 2015; adult measure, not households or every form of smartphone-only access.

test.reason: The bounded statistic or documentary statement is reported without assigning the cause of diffusion.

inference_limits: Mass emissions are not absorbed dose, disease or money damages. Old lead-flow factors, borrowed vehicle factors, load/lifespan assumptions and omitted processes prevent a full welfare estimate.

test.mechanism_chain: Battery manufacture/recycling and electricity use -> geographically redistributed pollution -> different lifecycle comparisons than tailpipe accounting.
test.strongest_rival: A vehicle without exhaust has negligible pollution regardless of energy/material supply chain or displaced travel.
test.discriminating_observation: Include lead flows and region-specific electricity; compare bicycle, bus, motorcycle and car rather than one favorable alternative.
test.evidence_sought_found: ENE-S13 performs a partial inventory and explicitly states missing health and lifecycle evidence.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Magnitude and exposure depend on process controls, region, service life and counterfactual travel; some inputs predate rapid e-bike expansion.

statement: African actors initiated or financed some southern roads as well as operating lorries: Heap records Kwahu contracting and the Begoro–Bosuso connection, while Austin identifies African demands, construction and ownership.

sources.supports: African road initiative and motor-lorry ownership/operation.
Named projects, chiefs, local resources, contractors and district-commissioner participation.

counterevidence: Colonial engineers, grants and contractors also contributed; official accounts celebrate cooperation.
inference_limits: Named initiative does not establish universal voluntariness, equal incidence of contributions, consent to land loss, or the proportion of roads independently initiated.

test.reason: Bounded report of inspected observations or evidence scope; no isolated causal effect is asserted.

statement: Southern lorries initially often fed railway long hauls and subsequently competed for cocoa freight; Austin reports rail export shares above 83% in 1922–23 and 58% in 1930–31, with head-loading commonly continuing from farms to local markets.

sources.locator: manuscript pp. 5–7, especially pp. 6–7 and notes 28, 30, 35–36
sources.supports: Timing, freight relationships, quoted modal shares and continued first-stage head-loading.

counterevidence: Road and rail continued to coexist; changes in commodities, surfaces, vehicles, policy and route selection accompany modal changes.
inference_limits: No complete adoption denominator, independent reconstruction of Cardinall’s series, or road-versus-rail welfare comparison. Do not join these shares to MOB-S08’s broad pre-1970 summary without reconciliation.

test.mechanism_chain: Lorry access to feeder routes complements cheap rail long hauls; improved road service and rates permit some direct coastal haulage -> changing freight shares.
test.strongest_rival: Changing cocoa geography, road quality, vehicle productivity and fiscal treatment can jointly account for modal shares; a share decline need not mean absolute rail contraction.
test.discriminating_observation: Matched route/season traffic and complete delivered costs before and after road improvement, separating new production from diverted rail loads.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read GHA-S01 pp. 5–7 for contemporary rates, feeder descriptions, export shares and retained farm-to-market head-loading; no matched route panel was available.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Aggregate temporal association does not isolate operating flexibility, physical improvements or institutional cost allocation.

statement: African owner-driver entry used smaller enterprises and, in some accounts, hire-purchase; contemporary reports attributed competitive success to low overheads and long working days, but the independent contribution of that business organization is not identified.

sources.supports: Chiefly fleets, smaller owners and 1927–28 administrative attribution of larger firms’ retreat.
Hire-purchase, owner-driver business, long workdays and contemporary profit descriptions.

counterevidence: The same growth coincided with different vehicles, roads, public expenditure and demand; reported owner profitability omits failures and unpaid time.
inference_limits: No ownership census, financing-contract sample, repayment/default series, driver hourly income or causal decomposition. Chiefly fleets and small owner-drivers are distinct actors.

test.mechanism_chain: Smaller ownership/operation units and hire-purchase -> entry with different overheads and financing -> observed expansion of African owner-drivers.
test.strongest_rival: Technical changes, state-funded roads, crop demand or reporting bias could explain the same expansion and large-firm exit.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable operator accounts including vehicle, routes, debt, upkeep, hours, failed firms and family work.
test.evidence_sought_found: GHA-S01 p. 7 and GHA-S02 pp. 34–35 document arrangements and contemporary attributions; they do not provide those matched accounts.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Low observed cash overhead could partly transfer costs into long or unpaid work and public road provision.

statement: Entry into the southern cocoa economy was mediated by differing land institutions: group purchases with extended credit in Akyem Abuakwa coexisted with predominantly leased access in Ashanti, with political authority shaping charges and terms.

sources.supports: Group finance and credit, sub-chief sales, Asante leases, stranger status and colonial intervention in rents.

counterevidence: Land suitability, scarcity, buyer migration, transaction size and timing also differ between the regions.
inference_limits: No matched causal estimate of political centralization; a farming-land credit arrangement is not evidence of a specific lorry-purchase loan.

test.mechanism_chain: Cocoa demand raises value of access -> buyers organize finance while authorities set sale/lease rules -> unequal and regionally different routes into cultivation.
test.strongest_rival: Different land availability, locations and stages of settlement could account for contract forms alongside political authority.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable transactions with land quality, buyer status, dates, chief authority, prices and access refusals.
test.evidence_sought_found: GHA-S01 pp. 15–17 supplies regional institutional contrasts, selected transactions and source limitations; no harmonized transaction dataset inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Historical political explanation is credible but not separated from regional economic differences.

statement: Austin links cocoa-farm income to expansion of hired labour and farm pledging while retaining early coerced farm work, continued compulsory road work, different forest/savanna opportunities and unequal gains by gender; transport enterprise did not imply a uniformly free surrounding labour system.

sources.locator: manuscript pp. 17–20, especially p. 18 n. 104 and p. 20 n. 115
sources.supports: Early bound labour in Ashanti cocoa planting, later hiring/pledging, road compulsion, migration and gender qualifications.

counterevidence: Legal abolition, colonial enforcement, crop revenues and workers’ alternatives changed together; the source describes gradual uneven transitions.
inference_limits: No claim that cocoa or lorries alone abolished slavery, that all later labour was free, or that wage employment gave every person better welfare. Much evidence inherits Austin’s book and earlier scholarship.

test.mechanism_chain: Mature cocoa farms generate purchasing power and collateral -> employers can hire and borrowers pledge farms -> some movement away from bound labour, uneven across people and tasks.
test.strongest_rival: Legal emancipation and enforcement could drive change independently, while coerced labour itself helped create the productive farms.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated individual contracts and exit choices across farm maturation, emancipation enforcement and wage alternatives, separated by sex/status.
test.evidence_sought_found: GHA-S01 pp. 17–20 explicitly distinguishes ordinances, coerced planting, subsequent revenues, continuing road obligations and gender limits.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Reciprocal causation and heterogeneous enforcement prevent an isolated technological-emancipation explanation.

statement: The 1925 Makongo wage/contract dispute and a June 1930 Savelugu instruction rejecting forced supply of PWD workers show local changes in paid recruitment before Britain’s 1931 convention ratification, without identifying the independent influence of international pressure or anticipatory policy change.

sources.locator: “The Transition from Paid Forced Labour to Paid Voluntary Labour on PWD Roads”, notes 50–52
sources.supports: Protest, commissioners’ response and dated Savelugu diary on recruitment.

counterevidence: Earlier international pressure and policy debate remain possible influences; compulsory cleaning/weeding continued on some PWD roads.
inference_limits: Chronology does not quantify how many workers could refuse, date a universal end of compulsion, or show that law and international pressure were irrelevant.

test.mechanism_chain: Chiefs contest terms and local officials change recruitment -> documented paid work offered without compulsory supply before formal ratification.
test.strongest_rival: Earlier international pressure or anticipated legal change influenced the same local officials; local adjustments need not have been independent of external debate.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated recruitment practice plus correspondence identifying officials’ prior information, pressure and reasons, comparing similarly exposed districts.
test.evidence_sought_found: GHA-S04 cites 1925 complaints/responses and reproduces the June 1930 diary; these establish the reported sequence but do not isolate local from prior external influences.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Original diaries not independently reopened, and implementation breadth, anticipatory effects and residual tasks remain unresolved.

statement: Pont Cháfer connects changes in northern PWD recruitment to maintenance demands and workers’ alternatives; the post-1929 fall in southern wages could make northern offers attractive without a general improvement in workers’ outside options.

sources.locator: “The Transition from Paid Forced Labour to Paid Voluntary Labour on PWD Roads”, notes 53–66
sources.supports: Motor traffic/maintenance pressures, regional wage comparisons, Depression timing, recruitment reports and residual obligatory cleaning.

counterevidence: Legislation, local official convictions, budgets and technical organization also changed; wages and voluntary recruitment are separate variables.
inference_limits: No matched payroll/recruitment dataset or aggregate welfare estimate. Ending compulsory supply in one task does not establish that all work on the same road became voluntary.

test.mechanism_chain: Higher maintenance demands and resistance to compulsion -> local wage/recruitment changes; falling southern wages -> a stronger northern paid labour supply.
test.strongest_rival: Legal/political reform and new finance could explain recruitment changes even without relative-wage changes; source selection may overstate a smooth transition.
test.discriminating_observation: Recruitment, refusals, sanctions, wages including food, road conditions and budgets by site before/after policy and labour-market changes.
test.evidence_sought_found: GHA-S04 provides dated disputes, wage evidence and recruitment reports; it also retains residual weeding obligations and PWD’s limited mileage.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The evidence supports several interacting contributions and no isolated causal share.

statement: Northern political-road labour changed unevenly: Kunkel identifies arrangements and mid-1930s budget assumptions preserving compulsion, while Pont Cháfer emphasizes earlier dissent, district payments and later grant-financed paid gangs; their evidence does not establish one uniform transition date or compulsory-labour rate.

sources.locator: pp. 464–471, especially p. 469 n. 89 and pp. 470–471
sources.supports: Administrative powers, subsidy assumption, official dissent and local wage-payment initiatives.

sources.locator: “Indirect Rule, Taxation, and Unpaid Forced Labour”, notes 69–95
sources.supports: Explicit engagement with Kunkel, divergent district practices, budgets, grants and later legislation.

counterevidence: Kunkel herself records dissent and local paid work; Pont Cháfer retains coercion and exceptions. They are not simple all-coerced versus all-free accounts.
inference_limits: Planned allocation, actual payment and voluntary acceptance are different measures. Exact archive overlap and the representativeness of selected districts are not audited; no countrywide adjudication is attempted.

test.mechanism_chain: Legal classifications and administrative powers can preserve coerced maintenance, while local opposition and finance can shift particular roads toward paid recruitment.
test.strongest_rival: A uniform strategy of preserving compulsion versus an earlier, locally differentiated transition; both can coexist on different roads or tasks.
test.discriminating_observation: Link the same road’s planned budget to actual payroll, recruitment order, complaints and sanctions across years; compare maintained and abandoned roads.
test.evidence_sought_found: GHA-S03’s 1935 subsidy calculation and GHA-S04’s district expenditure/payroll accounts bear on different stages and places; both also describe dissent.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The available excerpts do not convert these heterogeneous observations into a comparable labour-days denominator.

statement: In the Krachi–Salaga–Kpandai area, records of village requests in 1928 and later road initiatives and grants show farmers helping create feeder connections, while seeking materials, skilled work or government support they could not readily supply themselves.

sources.locator: “People’s Roads and Unpaid Voluntary Labour”, notes 100–109
sources.supports: Bajamse request, village-built connections, grants and requests for tools/bridges.

counterevidence: Officials and native authorities supplied assistance and administered funds; some earlier routes in the area had been made using forced labour.
inference_limits: Named initiatives do not establish all-household consent, universal access to grants, or that every local road was voluntary. Later oral testimony is not backdated to every interwar episode.

test.reason: Bounded report of inspected observations or evidence scope; no isolated causal effect is asserted.

statement: Pont Cháfer reports deterioration of the Bladjai feeder road after fuel shortages stopped exports in April 1945, consistent with maintenance responding to the usefulness of lorry access, but without isolating that mechanism.

sources.locator: “People’s Roads and Unpaid Voluntary Labour”, note 110 and surrounding discussion
sources.supports: Dated export interruption and reported road deterioration.

counterevidence: Weather, labour availability, wartime conditions and funding may also have changed; absence of exports is not itself proof that all prior labour was voluntary.
inference_limits: Single qualitative sequence, no comparable control road, no traffic or labour-time denominator and no estimate of revenue or household welfare.

test.mechanism_chain: Fuel interruption stops lorry exports -> immediate practical return to maintenance falls -> reported deterioration of the road.
test.strongest_rival: Weather, wartime labour shortages or funding changes caused both the export interruption and reduced maintenance; official reporting may omit those factors.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated fuel, traffic, maintenance, weather and labour records for Bladjai and comparable roads unaffected by the fuel interruption.
test.evidence_sought_found: GHA-S04 reports the April 1945 sequence from a contemporary district diary; no matched series inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Temporal order is informative but does not uniquely identify incentives or voluntariness.

statement: The GHA road/lorry history adds actor and institutional evidence to MOB-C04; it neither independently replicates nor by itself invalidates Jedwab–Moradi’s spatial railway estimates, whose historical discussion already draws on Austin and Hill.

sources.locator: January 2015 manuscript, §4.1 printed pp. 11–12 (southern cocoa-suitable sample), §5.1.3 printed p. 18 (Hill/Austin migration discussion), and references
sources.supports: Southern cocoa-suitable sample, spatial units and direct Austin/Hill references.
Road/rail relationships and inherited historical source chain.

counterevidence: Historical summaries about early lorries and rail cocoa shares do not align transparently across the sources and warrant separate reconciliation.
inference_limits: This is a comparison of evidence scope and lineage, not an econometric reanalysis, an assertion of invalid identification, or a full welfare verdict.

test.reason: Bounded report of inspected observations or evidence scope; no isolated causal effect is asserted.

statement: Agricola’s 1556 account presents human, animal and hydraulic mine-work choices together and includes repairable components and site access among practical considerations.

sources.locator: Book II pp. 31–33; Book VI pp. 171–185, especially replacement teeth p. 173 and staged pump pp. 184–185
sources.supports: Documents explicit technical choices and maintenance provisions in the treatise.

counterevidence: Texts and illustrations may describe exemplary arrangements rather than common practice.
inference_limits: Supports existence of described techniques and stated criteria, not measured prevalence, profitability or a universal choice rule.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: In sixteenth- and seventeenth-century central European mining, rod transmission extended the use of waterpower to pumps distant from the stream; non-steam engineering continued to change.

sources.supports: Compares crank-driven pumps, remote rods, balanced transmission and later depictions.

counterevidence: Introduction dates vary; some depicted machinery is ambiguous. Some applications remained tied to local hydrology.
inference_limits: No region-wide diffusion denominator. Adequate hydraulics delaying German steam adoption is a further hypothesis, not established by this claim.

test.mechanism_chain: Remote hydraulic resource -> construct rod linkage -> mechanical power reaches distant pumps -> expanded site choice.
test.strongest_rival: Static post-Agricola mining would predict little relevant configuration change; a weaker rival accepts change but denies cost advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Later mechanisms and installations absent from Agricola distinguish change; operating accounts are needed for cost advantage.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read Agricola and Multhauf (IND-S01/S02); latter compares remote rod/ balanced transmission and later depictions.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Configuration change is supported; diffusion rate and net advantage remain unresolved.

statement: Nuvolari’s Cornish comparison links early Newcomen use to tolerable fuel costs and the uptake of more fuel-efficient Watt engines to the expense of imported coal in Cornwall.

sources.supports: Contrasts fuel-intensive atmospheric engines and Cornish demand for fuel economy; documents Boulton and Watt deployments.

counterevidence: Engine cost, drainage needs, labour, maintenance and royalties also entered investment decisions.
inference_limits: An historically supported pathway, not isolated identification of coal prices; cheap energy did not characterise every successful steam market.

test.mechanism_chain: High fuel use plus local fuel price -> investor comparison -> fuel-saving design becomes more attractive -> Cornish deployment.
test.strongest_rival: Drainage demand or capital/engineering availability alone could yield deployment without a coal-price mechanism.
test.discriminating_observation: Matched engine choices and total costs across sites with comparable drainage but different delivered coal prices.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S03 pp. 10–12: coalfield/Cornish fuel contrast and condenser deployments; no matched-site experiment acquired.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Engine capability, finance and demand differ with geography.

statement: From 1811, Cornish engine reporting made performance and practices comparable across installations; Nuvolari interprets this information sharing and overlapping investment as supports for incremental improvement.

sources.supports: Describes Lean’s reporting, engineering competition and cost-book ownership.

counterevidence: High-pressure designs and new investment arrived concurrently; a slack period followed patent expiry before reporting began.
inference_limits: Does not estimate the reporting effect separately from investment, engineers, fuel prices or design changes; original engine reports not directly audited.

test.mechanism_chain: Comparable public engine reports -> engineer comparison and reputation -> incremental changes -> improved duty.
test.strongest_rival: New high-pressure designs and investment alone predict improving duty, even without disclosure.
test.discriminating_observation: Within comparable investment/design cohorts, reporting exposure predicts improvement; evidence of actual copying strengthens transmission.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S03 pp. 14–20: reporting intent, public comparisons, changing duty and shared ownership; original report series not audited.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Reporting, design, investment and district growth coincide.

statement: Watt’s fuel-saving royalties and patent enforcement generated documented conflict in Cornwall; Nuvolari argues that broad exclusion also obstructed rival steam development.

sources.supports: Describes royalty formula, disputes, Hornblower and post-expiry withdrawal of Cornish orders.

counterevidence: Patents and royalties may also have financed development and dissemination; cessation of monopoly was not followed by immediate technical progress.
inference_limits: The direction and magnitude of net patent effects remain disputed. Distinguish the documented dispute from the author’s wider innovation judgement.

test.mechanism_chain: Broad patent enforcement -> restricted rival development -> delayed adoption of alternatives.
test.strongest_rival: Patent rents finance development and disclosure; litigation may protect appropriation rather than reduce total innovation.
test.discriminating_observation: Blocked independently workable designs and post-restriction improvement controlling for engineering capacity; also evidence of R&D financed by rents.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S03 pp. 12–14: Hornblower dispute, royalties, order cessation and subsequent slack period.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Dispute is stronger evidence than net innovation effect; expiry alone did not produce immediate progress.

statement: In Crafts’s January 2002 reconstruction, steam contributed less than 0.01 percentage points per year to British labour-productivity growth before 1830, with a larger later contribution including railways.

sources.supports: Reports growth-accounting estimates and their stock/share assumptions.

counterevidence: Early engine stocks are incomplete and unmeasured enabling effects may not be captured by aggregate accounting.
inference_limits: An estimate from the inspected version, not a timeless consensus or evidence that steam was unnecessary at individual sites. No cross-era forecast is made.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Jonell and colleagues reconstruct unused waterpower potential across much of Britain alongside local constraints around Greater Manchester, and describe supplementary steam use in water-powered mills.

sources.locator: “Impact on the British textile industry”; hydropower and mill-census methods; abstract
sources.supports: Supports geographical heterogeneity and mixed-power operation.

counterevidence: Reservoir construction, ownership, transmission and industrial location could alter usable supply; theoretical national potential is not economically deployable capacity.
inference_limits: Partial-text inspection only; underlying model and supplements not rerun. Local scarcity does not identify why factories originally clustered there.

test.mechanism_chain: Local dependable water constraints -> mill seeks extra power -> steam supplement/replacement -> capacity expansion.
test.strongest_rival: Labour access/control or agglomeration could favour steam despite adequate water; national abundance predicts no shortage only if local access is ignored.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable mills/sites with usable flow versus scarce flow, plus seasonal output and expansion decisions.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S05 impact/method sections: local Manchester constraint alongside national potential and supplementary steam; compared IND-S06 coordination abstract.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Industrial clustering partly creates scarcity; reservoir costs, rights and labour conditions unresolved.

statement: Malm argues that large proposed reservoir schemes in the 1820s–1830s failed partly because their collective financing and coordination requirements conflicted with manufacturers’ arrangements.

sources.supports: Explicitly attributes non-realisation of reservoir schemes to coordination and collective funding.

counterevidence: Physical reliability, projected demand, land rights and cost assumptions are alternative or interacting explanations.
inference_limits: Abstract-only evidence: claim is about the author’s interpretation, not an independent finding that water was consistently cheaper or every proposed scheme feasible.

test.mechanism_chain: Shared reservoir requires funding and allocation -> manufacturers cannot coordinate -> proposed expansion not built.
test.strongest_rival: Projects may be physically unreliable or financially unattractive even under feasible collective governance.
test.discriminating_observation: Scheme correspondence and cost/flow evidence showing viable projects blocked specifically by coordination, compared with realised schemes.
test.evidence_sought_found: Searched full article; only IND-S06 author abstract acquired. It explicitly makes the coordination claim; scheme-level evidence not found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Both rivals fit non-building. Weak-access claim retained only as attributed hypothesis.

statement: Allen’s explanation assigns British mechanisation to labour being expensive relative to capital and energy, and subsequent wider diffusion to improvements that reduced other input requirements.

sources.supports: States the factor-price and later engineering-diffusion thesis directly.

counterevidence: Task-specific female wages, regional heterogeneity, skills, markets and political power complicate the aggregate comparison.
inference_limits: Attribution of a hypothesis; introductory excerpt does not validate Allen’s profitability calculations or universal foreign non-viability.

test.mechanism_chain: High relevant labour cost relative to machinery/energy -> expected cost saving -> investment in labour-saving inventions/adoption.
test.strongest_rival: Low-paid spinning labour, quality requirements and skill/market complements could motivate or constrain adoption independently.
test.discriminating_observation: Task- and location-matched wages, output quality and machine payback comparisons before invention, including nonadopters.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read Allen excerpt IND-S07 and archival-pay critique IND-S08; high-wage formulation is clear but spinner wage surge is challenged.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Allen’s underlying calculations and later responses not inspected; international and local wages use different comparisons.

statement: Humphries and Schneider’s reconstructed British hand-spinning pay does not show a general wage surge immediately before the spinning inventions; it challenges including these workers in an undifferentiated high-wage economy.

sources.supports: Documents archival construction, source-type differences and absence of the proposed sharp wage increase.

counterevidence: Cotton data are scarce, fibres and worker populations differ, and daily earnings involve time assumptions; Allen’s later rejoinders are not assessed here.
inference_limits: A challenge to a particular wage premise, not proof that factor prices never mattered or causal identification of quality control as the alternative motive.

test.mechanism_chain: Reconstructed pay by source type does not show the proposed general pre-invention surge -> weakens the proposed general wage-surge premise. This does not identify the marginal labour-cost return to a particular machine or exclude wage incentives.
test.strongest_rival: Samples overrepresent institutional/part-time low-output labour, concealing a high-wage commercial cotton margin.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable full-time commercial cotton spinning records with counts and hours, versus institutional and other fibres.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S08 source definitions, records and regressions: no general surge, source-type gaps, sparse cotton observations; explicit limits preserved.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Wage levels, wage changes, daily earnings, hourly labour costs and returns to a particular machine are different measures. Sparse commercial cotton records and working-time assumptions leave the relevant marginal incentive unresolved; alternative invention motives in IND-S08 remain speculative.

statement: In 1835 Ure publicly advocated factory mechanisation partly as a means to substitute cheaper labour and reduce dependence on independent skilled workers.

sources.locator: extract paragraphs beginning “The principle of the factory system”, “By the infirmity”, and “In the infancy of mechanical engineering”; compiler original-page ranges 20–23, 29–31
sources.supports: Records contemporary managerial advocacy for skill substitution and tractability.

counterevidence: Skilled mechanics and machine operatives remained necessary; Ure is a partisan advocate whose welfare claims are not corroborated by this extract.
inference_limits: Shows a stated aspiration, not universal employer intention, successful complete deskilling or demonstrated worker benefit.

test.reason: The bounded claim identifies a text, configuration, attributed estimate or observed dataset measure; it does not estimate the causes of the wider outcome. See inference_limits for the distinction.

statement: Kelly and Ó Gráda trace a pathway from instrument-making skill and precision measurement to complex textile machinery and the machine tools needed for repeated production and replacement parts.

sources.supports: Identifies skill transfer, gauges and exact tools, and the demand for reproducible wearing components.

counterevidence: The jenny and atmospheric engine could use less elaborate capabilities; cross-country tool histories have other routes and political contingencies.
inference_limits: A historically supported pathway rather than a universal prerequisite; no independent causal effect of national skill endowment is estimated.

test.mechanism_chain: Precision craft/measurement capabilities -> reproducible complicated components -> machinery supply and replacement -> sustained industrial use.
test.strongest_rival: Demand/capital expansion alone induces both tool skill and machinery; capabilities could be an outcome rather than prior constraint.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated personnel/tool transfers preceding new workable designs and matched sites with demand but missing skills.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S10 sections 2.1–2.3: named instrument/mechanic transfers, valve making and machine-tool/parts account; also simpler early artifacts acknowledged.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Demand and supply reinforce one another; broad national claims lack an exogenous comparison.

statement: Broadberry and Gupta’s reconstruction makes the timing of Lancashire’s competitive gains depend on raw-cotton and transport costs as well as wages and uneven productivity advances across spinning and weaving.

sources.supports: Reconstructs comparative wages, productivity proxies, raw cotton prices and market-specific delivery costs.

counterevidence: Indian productivity stagnation is assumed for key intervals, and household earnings and labour units are not directly comparable; political market access remains a rival/complement.
inference_limits: Applies to the inspected 2005 model and reconstruction, not directly measured productivity for all Indian textiles or proof of tariffs’ irrelevance.

test.mechanism_chain: Productivity rises unevenly and cotton/freight costs change -> relative delivered cost shifts -> merchants source differently -> competitive reversal.
test.strongest_rival: Colonial policy and coercive market access could drive the same trade shifts without equivalent cost advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Quality-matched delivered costs and shares across markets with different policy but similar transport, before and after price changes.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S11 pp. 16–25 and conclusion; compared IND-S13 policy testimony. The cost model includes cotton/freight but assumes some Indian productivity paths.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Policy shapes prices and markets; quality and labour-unit comparability remain incomplete.

statement: Clingingsmith and Williamson propose that pre-1810 Indian textile decline involved domestic political/agricultural shocks, while later decline involved stronger international manufactured-price pressure.

sources.supports: Uses a three-sector model and relative-price evidence to propose two phases.

counterevidence: Regional political histories and data are uneven; colonial intervention, quality changes and capital constraints are not independently isolated by these prices.
inference_limits: Model assumptions include mobile labour, subsistence-linked pay and initially non-traded grain. This is an interpretation, not exogenous identification of drought or Mughal decline.

test.mechanism_chain: Domestic agricultural/political shock -> dear grain and subsistence-linked nominal wages -> reduced textile competitiveness; later world textile prices add pressure.
test.strongest_rival: Colonial interventions or textile demand shifts could alter prices and employment without the posited agricultural cause.
test.discriminating_observation: District timing: independently measured harvest/drought/conflict shocks preceding wage pressure and textile contraction, including low-shock controls.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S12 model and relative-price/timing argument; no independently identified district treatment comparison found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Modelled labour mobility and wage linkage do causal work; price data alone fit multiple mechanisms.

statement: Inikori argues that Atlantic demand linked to slavery-based commodity production helped form the markets and regional expansion within which British cotton mechanisation developed.

sources.locator: sections I–III, especially section II paragraphs on Lancashire’s wages and Atlantic export sales
sources.supports: Connects regional protoindustry, Atlantic demand and later mechanisation.

counterevidence: Factor prices, domestic demand, engineering and other trading regions also matter; regional wage rankings do not by themselves adjudicate international wage comparisons.
inference_limits: An attributed historical mechanism, not a quantified necessary contribution of slavery to each invention. Export demand is not the same variable as investment finance.

test.mechanism_chain: Slavery-linked Atlantic commodity trade -> expanding markets -> regional protoindustry growth -> investment and mechanisation incentives.
test.strongest_rival: Domestic markets, factor prices or engineering can explain innovation; Atlantic demand might follow rather than precede industrial advantage.
test.discriminating_observation: Regional/sectoral demand exposure preceding investment, with comparable low-exposure producers and separate supply/finance channels.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read IND-S13 regional wage/exports sequence and IND-S11 competition account; temporal market linkage found, no isolated necessity test.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Atlantic markets, shipping, wages and political power are reciprocally connected; export shares are not investment causality.

statement: Inikori’s discussion of Charles Grant’s 1821 testimony identifies asymmetric British and Indian tariff power as a contemporary concern alongside improvements in machinery.

sources.locator: section IV, Charles Grant paragraph immediately preceding table 3
sources.supports: Reproduces an explicit contemporary argument about protection at home and political power over Indian imports.

counterevidence: The testimony does not establish a tariff counterfactual for each cloth quality or exclude cost-driven competitive shifts.
inference_limits: Primary testimony is accessed through Inikori’s quotation via Chaudhuri; original parliamentary record not independently inspected. No causal magnitude assigned.

test.mechanism_chain: Imperial tariff authority -> asymmetric protection/import permission -> altered producer choice set and market access.
test.strongest_rival: Productivity and freight advantages alone would produce the same import shift under symmetric sovereignty.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable products under differing tariff regimes and original legislative/merchant records on excluded choices.
test.evidence_sought_found: Read Grant testimony as reproduced in IND-S13 section IV; sought original-record specificity but did not acquire parliamentary source.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Testimony establishes awareness and constrained sovereignty more firmly than the counterfactual trade magnitude.

statement: Japanese mills in the 1890s adapted ring spinning through a package involving cotton imports, mixed fibres, more preparation labour and a changed labour force, rather than merely copying American operating conditions.

sources.supports: Combines order specifications with historical accounts of cotton preparation and workforce change.

counterevidence: Cotton prices, yarn markets and suppliers changed concurrently; order specifications are not direct measurements of realised mill productivity.
inference_limits: Does not establish the separate effect of each component, or that the labour arrangements were freely chosen or beneficial to workers.

statement: Early eighteenth-century reports connect British variolation discussions to Ottoman practitioners, including women, and African expertise conveyed through Onesimus; this is evidence of transmission rather than a British origin.

statement: Lister’s 1867 address presented an evolving wound-treatment practice through cases and claimed ward improvements, rather than a controlled trial of a fixed protocol.

sources.locator: Statistics; Glasgow Royal Infirmary; Longer-term perspective

sources.supports: Traces demonstrations, hands-on details, students and adaptation.

statement: Alsan and Goldin estimate that combined safe water and effective sewerage account for about one-third of the decline in log under-five mortality in their jointly treated Massachusetts municipalities, 1880–1920; the interventions are complementary in their preferred model.

statement: Wartime penicillin supply required solving culture-yield and downstream-processing problems in addition to establishing clinical promise.

sources.supports: Scale-up, extraction, purification and sterile production.
Culture medium and strain work.

counterevidence: Institutional accounts may overstate their own component's contribution.
inference_limits: Process-specific contribution, not proof that this exact route was the only possible route.

test.discriminating_observation: Measured yields and losses before/after controlled process changes
test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S09/S10 describe process improvements and production transition; no primary batch logs inspected
test.remaining_ambiguity: Causal weights and alternative industrial routes remain unresolved.

statement: Pfizer’s prior submerged-fermentation experience was an identified contributor to its penicillin production route.

sources.supports: Connects gluconic-acid process knowledge to penicillin tanks.

counterevidence: Capital, procurement access and new staff might matter as much as inherited skills.

test.strongest_rival: Capital and purchasing incentives could account for success despite different prior experience

test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S09 names a concrete technical transfer; no matched firm histories examined
test.remaining_ambiguity: Source may organize history retrospectively around eventual success.

statement: Governmental coordination and firms’ investment choices accompanied penicillin scale-up, while committing plant capacity involved opportunity costs.

sources.locator: Opening; Penicillin Production by Deep-tank Fermentation
sources.supports: Government approach to firms and risk of curtailing other products.
Public laboratory/industrial connection.

test.evidence_sought_found: MED-S09/S10 document collaboration and resource commitment, not the counterfactual financing path
test.remaining_ambiguity: Correlation with wartime effort does not establish unique necessity.

statement: Sri Lankan records reported six indigenous and eleven imported malaria cases in 1963, followed by reduced control activity and a major late-1960s resurgence.

sources.locator: Weakening of the malaria control programme, Sri Lanka paragraph

counterevidence: Both accounts inherit overlapping historical records.
inference_limits: Case counts depend on detection; sequence alone is not a causal estimate.

test.reason: Records temporal pattern and reported classifications without allocating causal shares.

statement: For pottery movement in lowland Britain c. 250–400 CE, Wiseman and colleagues infer best-fit road costs roughly three times river and four times sea costs, with wide uncertainty and regional river variation.

test.mechanism_chain: Additional transfers/access legs incur resources -> total delivery cost differs from line-haul price -> ranking inferred from a segment may change.
test.strongest_rival: Sea advantages remain dominant because transfer costs are negligible relative to long line-haul savings.
test.discriminating_observation: Observe or reconstruct full chains at different distances; whether adding transfers changes relative delivered cost distinguishes claims for a particular route.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S02 explicitly enumerates omitted costs and derives different end-to-end ratios; MOB-S01 acknowledges schematic price calibration.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The existence of omitted terms is established, but no universal ranking reversal is demonstrated.

statement: Inka expansion incorporated earlier Andean routes and added or maintained roads, stores and wayside facilities, so imperial scaling was partly the integration of inherited infrastructure.

statement: For Garrido’s Cachiyuyo de Llampos road segment in the Atacama, water and forage scarcity make predominantly pedestrian traffic more plausible than regular llama caravans.

statement: At Cachiyuyo de Llampos, settlement, craft and roadside assemblages support Garrido’s interpretation that some local miners used the Inka Road for exchange beyond directly administered state production.

statement: Early private Indian railway expansion combined British capital with colonial guarantees, while government line-placement priorities included military control; observed construction was not simply a market vote by passengers or farmers.

statement: Donaldson’s published study finds lower trade costs and higher trade, and estimates a 0.164 log-point rise in real agricultural income per unit area following rail access in its district panel; the paper summarizes the income effect as about 16%.

statement: Bogart and Chaudhary find lower working expenses after colonial state takeovers of Indian railways, with employment reductions supporting a labour-cost channel; they do not directly observe railway wages.

test.mechanism_chain: Contractual state purchase strengthens treasury incentive -> labour/input reorganization -> lower employment/expenses.

statement: The April 2019 accepted manuscript by Bogart and Chaudhary estimates average annual total returns of 3.7% on Indian guaranteed railway securities for 1880–1908 and finds no average abnormal returns in the three years before state purchases.

statement: The Ghanaian western railway was routed toward gold mines and Kumasi for commercial and military purposes, while the eastern route had different political and commercial origins and reached Kumasi only in 1923 after wartime delays.

sources.supports: Reconstructs western line Sekondi–Tarkwa–Obuasi–Kumasi and eastern Accra route, lobbying, governors and construction dates.

counterevidence: Alternative surveyed routes were judged attractive for agriculture; cocoa potential was already relevant to the eastern line.
inference_limits: Mainly the authors’ historical reconstruction; colonial political interests and technical transport benefits are not mutually exclusive.

test.reason: Bounded documentary/model/measurement statement; does not itself estimate a causal contribution. Associated causal propositions are tested separately.

statement: Jedwab and Moradi find that railway access encouraged cocoa production and settlement growth in Ghana, using geographic controls, planned-but-unbuilt lines and instruments to address route selection.

sources.supports: Spatial data and identification exercises compare rail areas with controls and placebo routes.

counterevidence: The eastern line could partly respond to cocoa prospects; instruments rely on exclusion assumptions and local growth can include relocation.
inference_limits: This is the January 2015 forthcoming version. Effects on cells and towns do not by themselves identify household gains or a full national cost-benefit balance.

test.mechanism_chain: Rail access lowers inland shipment costs -> farmers expand cocoa -> rural production supports trading towns.
test.strongest_rival: Planners selected inherently promising cocoa areas and pre-existing settlement growth rather than causing expansion.
test.discriminating_observation: Effects absent near comparable planned-but-unbuilt lines, stronger with actual access, and robust to alternative alignments would count against simple selection.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S08 §4 and Table 3 compare planned routes, geographic controls and straight-line instruments; paper reports rail effects and weak placebo effects for Ghana.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Instrument exclusion is substantive; political endpoint choice and cocoa suitability can still correlate with unobserved potential.

statement: Ghanaian railway traffic declined sharply after 1974, yet towns near former railway routes retained relative economic importance through the study’s 2000 endpoint as roads expanded.

sources.supports: Rail decline, near-route road replacement, and persistence results; authors discuss sunk investments and coordination.

counterevidence: Roads preserved absolute transport access; persistence does not show towns could flourish with no replacement transport.
inference_limits: Not a claim about current Ghanaian railways. Sunk capital, continuing amenities and expectation-based coordination are difficult to fully disentangle.

test.mechanism_chain: Early rail connection concentrates settlement/investment -> subsequent actors coordinate around established towns -> relative concentration persists after rail traffic declines.
test.strongest_rival: Persistent geography, road replacement or unmeasured durable amenities explain persistence without expectation-based coordination.
test.discriminating_observation: Persistence after equalized access and controls for inherited assets supports coordination; direct evidence of investors following prior settlement rather than amenities would be stronger.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S08 §6 controls for roads and historical facilities and discusses population persistence. Authors explicitly note possible mismeasurement of sunk assets and instrument caveats.
test.remaining_ambiguity: The fall of rail does not remove roads or all place advantages; evidence supports persistence more strongly than a uniquely identified coordination mechanism.

statement: The same Ghana study describes a feedback between poor service, lower freight revenue and deferred maintenance, alongside cocoa cultivation’s movement into new forest areas, as context for rail decline.

sources.supports: Historical description links deficits/service/maintenance and changing cocoa geography; forests converted to cocoa and later food crops.

counterevidence: Political instability, roads, changing labour costs and management also mattered.
inference_limits: The paper does not separately identify the causal contribution of each decline mechanism or quantify net deforestation, deaths, dispossession or environmental welfare.

test.mechanism_chain: Service/financial deterioration and shifting crop geography -> lower rail demand/revenue -> deferred repair -> further deterioration.
test.strongest_rival: Road competition or political mismanagement alone caused decline, with maintenance and crop shifts mainly consequences.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated line-level service, finance, repair and commodity-flow series could establish ordering and distinguish shocks.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S08 §2.2 provides historical sequence and mechanisms, including forest-to-cocoa shifts, but no separate causal decomposition was inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Feedback makes direction reciprocal; environmental net costs are not identified.

statement: The 1897 New York electric-cab venture deliberately sold transport service while retaining vehicles and specialist control, rather than merely selling cars to inexperienced owners; operation was demonstrated before profitability was established.

sources.supports: Morris and Salom’s service model, operating experience and initial-cost assessment.

counterevidence: The first six months were probably loss-making on Kirsch’s reconstruction, and reported operation is not proof of scalable profitability.
inference_limits: Operational results were originally self-reported and the profitability inference uses later cost studies; this contribution does not reproduce the implied cost calculation.

test.reason: Bounded documentary/model/measurement statement; does not itself estimate a causal contribution. Associated causal propositions are tested separately.

statement: Kirsch’s history attributes the EVC’s breakdown to a bundle of production, financial and organizational problems, and distinguishes early operating-company failures from the parent’s default in December 1907.

sources.supports: Production delays, fires, shareholder suits, public attacks, regional failures and later parent default.

counterevidence: Battery limitations and unreliable vehicles remain part of the contemporary feasibility problem; business failure does not prove a viable alternative would otherwise have won.
inference_limits: Author dissertation summary; relative weights of factors are not independently identified. A successful EVC counterfactual is not an observed outcome.

test.mechanism_chain: Ambitious system expansion encounters operational/financial problems -> operating firms fail -> organizational collapse damages the service model.
test.strongest_rival: Battery shortcomings alone made profitable service impossible, so financial trouble was simply a downstream symptom.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable fleets with sound finance but similar batteries, plus separated operating/financing accounts, would test sufficiency of the battery explanation.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S09 p. 307 documents several failure modes; MOB-S10 shows later task-specific viable fleets, weakening a timeless impossibility claim but not isolating EVC causes.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Later fleets had improved batteries and different tasks; sources share some intellectual lineage; no clean comparison quantifies causal weights.

statement: Mom’s comparative history distinguishes early battery-related failures from later electric fleets that worked under specific duty cycles and disciplined maintenance; it rejects the electric starter as a sufficient explanation for all electric-vehicle displacement.

sources.supports: Discusses sulphation/maintenance, commercial and specialized fleets, universal gasoline use and starter timing.

counterevidence: The gasoline vehicle’s range, autonomy and purchase cost were real advantages for general private use; fleet successes were conditional.
inference_limits: US-focused case with European task contrasts. No all-vehicle market share or claim of equivalent generalized performance; interpretation translated from German.

test.mechanism_chain: Duty cycle and disciplined maintenance mitigate battery weaknesses -> specified fleet work remains viable -> general private-car displacement coexists with electric niches.
test.strongest_rival: One universally inferior propulsion technology or the 1912 starter alone explains all electric decline.
test.discriminating_observation: Successful electric tasks after the starter and differing decline by application contradict a universal single-trigger prediction.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S10 pp. 281–283 identifies successful defined fleets and notes the Model T starter appeared in 1919; source explicitly disaggregates generations/tasks.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Fleet success does not establish equal suitability for touring or lower costs for every owner; the broad interpretation is historical, not an experiment.

statement: The Electric Vehicle Association of America, established in 1909, promoted utility fleets, charging facilities, off-peak rates and a common charging plug; this was an organized attempt to build complements after early electric-car setbacks.

sources.supports: Formation, membership, marketing and standard-plug committee, then incorporation into NELA in 1916.

counterevidence: Central stations were not uniformly supportive, and coordination alone did not remove battery and vehicle costs.
inference_limits: Earlier coordination changing the dominant technology is Kirsch’s counterfactual hypothesis, not a causal result established here.

test.reason: Bounded documentary/model/measurement statement; does not itself estimate a causal contribution. Associated causal propositions are tested separately.

statement: Postwar container scaling required compatible handling equipment and intermodal facilities; the published trade study distinguishes 1956 US commercial deployment from the start of its international diffusion period in 1966.

sources.supports: Specialized cranes, road/rail/ship integration, Ideal-X deployment and international standardization narrative.

counterevidence: Earlier containers and domestic experiments existed; some goods and routes remained outside containerization.
inference_limits: Dates describe this study’s modern container-system convention, not invention of boxes or the first transport container anywhere.

test.mechanism_chain: Compatible boxes and equipment reduce repeated handling -> ship/rail/truck interfaces work together -> deployments can scale beyond one proprietary route.
test.strongest_rival: A better ship or cheaper box alone explains diffusion without complementary investment.
test.discriminating_observation: Early experiments that failed with weak handling complements, followed by adoption tied to cranes/terminals/standards, discriminate against artifact-only explanations.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S11 §§2.1–2.3 reports prewar experiments, specialized-capital constraints, early port reluctance and negotiated compatibility.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Narrative is inherited from earlier histories; it does not prove any one exact standard or institutional arrangement was necessary.

statement: US construction subsidies tied to approved container dimensions, international standardization and military logistics demand in the Vietnam War helped create conditions for container diffusion; these were distinct from intrinsic box efficiency.

sources.supports: Federal Maritime Board policy, ISO compromises and military logistics described as complementary mechanisms.

counterevidence: The historical narrative also starts with private shipping investment; it does not identify military demand as necessary for every route.
inference_limits: Historical interpretation in an econometric paper, based on prior histories. No causal estimate of each policy or claim that war was necessary for global containerization.

test.mechanism_chain: Subsidy specifications/ISO coordination and military demand -> reduce compatibility/investment uncertainty and add traffic -> support diffusion.
test.strongest_rival: Commercial demand and private integrated shipping would have produced the same diffusion trajectory without these policies.
test.discriminating_observation: Route- and firm-level investment responses to policy changes, or comparable commercial routes without military demand, would separate contribution from coincidence.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S11 p. 40 documents the historical policy and procurement channels; no dedicated causal estimate of their incremental effect is provided.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Military demand, private innovation and standardization interacted; narrative timing cannot identify necessity.

statement: Bernhofen and colleagues warn that very large estimates using adoption dates alone do not convincingly establish causal trade effects; their product-containerizability comparisons are smaller and provide stronger but still qualified support.

sources.supports: Pre-trend failures and endogeneity warning; benchmark 17.4% North–North product differential and approximately 14% world differential with delayed accrual.

counterevidence: Classification and robustness choices alter estimated magnitudes; product-level effects do not capture every network spillover.
inference_limits: Do not quote old working-paper 700% figures as established causal effects. Denominators are bilateral product trade comparisons over specified periods, not total global GDP or a universal return to a container port.

test.mechanism_chain: Container systems lower relevant handling costs -> suitable products should gain more trade than unsuitable products after adoption.
test.strongest_rival: Countries adopt while trade is already growing, inflating aggregate adoption-timing effects.
test.discriminating_observation: Pre-adoption trends among future adopters and suitable/unsuitable products test timing confounding; comparative product responses add a discriminating dimension.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S11 p. 37 explicitly reports failed parallel-trend robustness for adoption-only models. Tables 2–3 and pp. 44–46 give smaller product differentials and classification sensitivity.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Suitability definitions and correlated product shocks remain; product effects are not equivalent to all general-equilibrium benefits.

statement: The 1960 West Coast mechanization agreement exchanged union acceptance of labour-saving changes for a $29 million fund over 1961–1966, and its financing imposed uneven charges contested by Volkswagen.

sources.supports: Agreement, fund, and weight-versus-volume assessment dispute.

counterevidence: A negotiated fund does not establish that every worker or shipper was compensated, nor that all members regarded the terms as fair.
inference_limits: Court record of specific contracts and litigated incidence; not an aggregate estimate of gains or proof that containers alone caused every negotiated change.

test.reason: Bounded documentary/model/measurement statement; does not itself estimate a causal contribution. Associated causal propositions are tested separately.

statement: Containerization shifted much stuffing and unstuffing away from docks, creating conflict between longshore and Teamster jurisdictions after the initial West Coast mechanization bargain.

sources.locator: part I, paragraphs describing break-bulk, 1960 agreement and off-dock container work
sources.supports: Court recounts Board findings of greater-than-expected work loss and the dispute over a fifty-mile work-preservation agreement.

counterevidence: Some longshore workers acquired new container-handling roles; moving tasks is not equivalent to eliminating all employment.
inference_limits: Judicial retrospective of a particular dispute, not a comprehensive labour census. Legal characterization of work restrictions is not adopted as a neutral welfare assessment.

test.mechanism_chain: Sealed intermodal boxes bypass repeated dock handling -> stuffing/unstuffing moves inland -> occupational jurisdiction is contested.
test.strongest_rival: Work loss consists only of machine substitution, with no material relocation across employers or unions.
test.discriminating_observation: Observed off-dock stuffing by Teamsters and disputes over those tasks distinguish relocation from pure disappearance.
test.evidence_sought_found: MOB-S13 part I recounts off-dock work and the fifty-mile supplement litigation, alongside new dockside equipment duties.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Court evidence cannot count net jobs or infer conditions at every freight station.

statement: Goh Chok Tong’s 2000 terminal-opening speech records Singapore’s 1972 container berths and presents further port expansion as a coordinated choice involving scarce waterfront land, long planning horizons, workforce upgrading and information services.

sources.supports: 1972 chronology and official explanation of Pasir Panjang land, capacity and service choices.

counterevidence: The official account celebrates success and omits a full account of displaced uses, residents and environmental costs.
inference_limits: Strong evidence of publicly stated state rationale, weaker evidence of exclusive causes of success; no independent causal estimate and no use of the speech’s forecasts.

test.reason: Bounded documentary/model/measurement statement; does not itself estimate a causal contribution. Associated causal propositions are tested separately.

statement: Bloom's historical synthesis places papermaking in Baghdad by the late eighth century and its transmission to Mediterranean Christians by the twelfth; this is a broad chronology of manufacture, not a unique invention event.

sources.locator: pp. 51–54, The Early Diffusion of Papermaking and The Replacement of Papyrus and Parchment
sources.supports: Manufacturing and transfer chronology; paper use predates European typography.

counterevidence: Regional practice and surviving evidence are uneven; exact first mills and routes are less secure than the broad sequence.
inference_limits: Does not establish a single battle-mediated transfer, rates of uptake, literacy effects, or indigenous manufacturing wherever paper was used.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: For the high-quality European book/writing-paper workflow reconstructed for 1300–1800, water quality, fibre preparation and gelatin sizing affected usable sheet properties; a generic recipe for pulp did not capture the complete craft.

sources.locator: Introduction; Raw Materials/Water; Sizing, paragraphs beginning As a result and Gelatin size allowed
sources.supports: Production constraints, sizing function, practical and historical evidential limits.
Storage, provenance and material-classification limits prevent a simple cross-regional superiority inference.

counterevidence: Barrett explicitly calls aspects reconstruction/hypothesis; climatic storage and survival also affect present condition.
inference_limits: No quantified contribution to historical costs, output or regional adoption; high-quality European paper is not all paper.

test.mechanism_chain: Controlled inputs and finishing -> workable, ink-resistant sheets -> suitability for specific writing/printing tasks
test.strongest_rival: Observed surviving-paper quality could instead reflect storage and preservation selection; cheaper rough paper could satisfy other tasks.
test.discriminating_observation: Matched historical papers or workshop records separating manufacture from storage and end-use requirements.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S02 was read for process evidence; NET-S03 explicitly warns that unknown storage prevents general causal claims about stability.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Technical functionality is supported; contribution to historical diffusion and cross-regional cost differences remains unidentified.

statement: Bloom cites Italian watermarked paper used in a Tunisian royal letter in 1350 and a 1409 Ibn Marzuq ruling permitting writing on Christian-made paper with objectionable watermark imagery; imported paper could support local writing without local manufacture.

sources.locator: pp. 63–64, Trade Relations and the Decline of Arab Papermaking
sources.supports: Specific imported-paper examples and the permissive ruling.

counterevidence: The ruling records a normative solution, not the subsequent number of purchasers; imports and local production could coexist.
inference_limits: Underlying letter and fatwa not directly inspected. Does not prove imports were always cheaper or that ruling caused a measured increase.

test.mechanism_chain: Imported sheets encounter religious objections -> jurist authorises their use -> a permissible route to continued local writing
test.strongest_rival: Material availability or price alone determines purchases; the ruling retrospectively validates an already established practice.
test.discriminating_observation: Purchasing changes before/after the ruling or correspondence showing objections prevented use until resolved.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S01 reports both actual imported-paper use and the later ruling; no before/after purchase series was found.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Chronological sequence demonstrates compatibility of religion and adoption, but not the ruling's marginal effect on demand.

statement: Mahgoub et al.'s 228-paper collection includes 133 undated samples and mostly eighteenth-/nineteenth-century dated examples; text language and finishing cannot by themselves establish paper's place of manufacture.

sources.locator: pp. 2–3, discussion before Methods and Reference collection
sources.supports: Sample composition, uncertain provenance, trade and finishing complications.

counterevidence: Some watermarks, fibres and morphology can inform provenance when combined with other evidence.
inference_limits: The study supplies no medieval adoption curve and no representative comparison of Islamic and European production efficiency.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: The surviving 868 Diamond Sutra's translated colophon names Wang Jie and a distribution dedication for his parents; it documents sponsored woodblock production and declared purpose, not achieved circulation volume.

sources.locator: The Diamond Sutra; Colophon from the Diamond Sutra (object Or.8210/P.2)
sources.supports: Date, printing method, sponsorship and declared distribution purpose.

counterevidence: This is a surviving dated object rather than the earliest-ever experiment; no run count is preserved in the cited description.
inference_limits: Institutionally translated colophon, not independent original-language collation. Purpose does not demonstrate that universal distribution occurred.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: Shen Gua describes Bi Sheng's clay-type process in 1041–1048, including type levelling, multiple common characters and alternating boards; he reports greater convenience for many copies than a few.

sources.locator: appendix 3, pp. 22–24, movable-type passage and nn. 69–71
sources.supports: Operational description and the author's conditional efficiency assessment.

counterevidence: Clay composition and later interpretations are debated; the passage does not supply timed trials or a surviving print-run account.
inference_limits: High confidence is in what the text reports, not an independently verified cost advantage or mass adoption.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: McDermott and Burke identify spatially and temporally separable craft stages, reusable blocks and thin-paper use as advantages of Chinese woodblock production relative to European press-room organisation.

sources.supports: Division of labour, later reprinting from blocks, paper/premises and financing comparisons.

counterevidence: Blocks required skilled cutting and storage; costs differed by quality, wage and place. No matched workshop price panel is supplied.
inference_limits: Conditional production affordances do not prove universal woodblock cheapness or economic optimality.

test.mechanism_chain: Separable stages and retained blocks -> flexible labour scheduling and later reprints -> viable decentralised publishing
test.strongest_rival: Woodblock persistence mainly follows script size, restrictions or lack of capital, even when workflows are inefficient.
test.discriminating_observation: Same-script publishers switching methods with demand volatility, reprint interval or relative labour prices.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S05 documents workflow differences and movable-type niches, while NET-S04 already distinguishes print-run scales.
test.remaining_ambiguity: These observations weaken technological-incapacity stories but do not isolate cost from institutions or preferences.

statement: Chinese movable-type use in particular genealogical and imperial projects coexisted with predominant woodblock printing in 1450–1850; a writing system alone is insufficient to specify which method was used for every task.

sources.supports: Woodblock predominance alongside explicitly identified movable-type niches.
Early process testimony and later predominance distinction.
Cost-model compatibility with the same genealogical and imperial niches.

counterevidence: Angeles’s script-sensitive cost model predicts block predominance and type niches using pages, print runs and type material; fitting those inherited observations does not identify script’s causal weight.
inference_limits: Niches reject practical impossibility and a uniform all-tasks rule, not a script-sensitive cost explanation of limited relative uptake. Relative causal weights remain unestablished.

test.mechanism_chain: Different production tasks and input costs within a script -> differing method choices -> persistent woodblock/type coexistence
test.strongest_rival: Script-sensitive fixed and operating costs, combined with print runs and pages, predict the observed niches without an independently identified institutional effect.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable projects with measured composition, storage and reprint costs, or a type-cost change within one market, could separate predictions. Niche existence alone cannot.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S05 describes niches; NET-S16 explicitly models them. Thus the alleged counterexample does not discriminate against this stronger rival.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Historical calibration, demand and project selection remain uncertain. Categorical impossibility is excluded; explanation of relative use is unresolved.

statement: The BnF identifies its surviving Jikji volume as metal-type printing from Heungdeok-sa in 1377 and records a complete woodblock version from 1378; the evidence shows adjacent uses, not replacement or mass readership.

sources.locator: What is Jikji?; A treasure of humanity; Preservation and access
sources.supports: Techniques, dates and partial survival of BnF volume.

counterevidence: Only part of the metal-type edition survives in this holding; run sizes and reader counts are unknown.
inference_limits: Do not equate oldest known surviving object with first invention, profitable reproduction or economy-wide diffusion.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: Park's synthesis places elite female/palace manuscript circulation of Korean vernacular novels in the late seventeenth century and commercial rental manuscripts from the mid-eighteenth, with continued coexistence of later woodblock versions.

sources.locator: pp. 22–24, The Chosŏn Book World Beyond Print
sources.supports: Chronology, audiences, rental circulation and warning against a replacement sequence.

counterevidence: Vernacular genres and audiences differed; surviving evidence is not a population-wide readership sample.
inference_limits: Commercial circulation is not necessarily print. No inference of national literacy growth, reader numbers or universal female access.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: Late Chosŏn copying served access to imported books and literary collections, including selected or variant texts; manuscript publication cannot be treated solely as a preliminary stage awaiting print.

sources.locator: pp. 25–28, imported Chinese books, literary collections and Toward More Descriptions
sources.supports: Copying practices, selective texts, publication without expected printing and variable reading contexts.

counterevidence: High prices or limited printed supply may still explain particular copied texts; textual change need not be deliberate preference.
inference_limits: No aggregate cost advantage or mental preference inferred from manuscript survival alone.

test.mechanism_chain: Demand for newly obtained or tailored texts -> scribal duplication/selection -> circulation without waiting for a print edition
test.strongest_rival: Copying persists only because otherwise identical printed books are expensive or unavailable.
test.discriminating_observation: Manuscripts that selectively rework printed sources, circulate for specific readers or are prepared without expectation of printing.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S08 pp. 25–28 documents such practices and contrasts them with print-centred generalisations.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Tailoring, affordability and shortage can operate together; relative importance remains unmeasured.

statement: Park cites private publishing drawing on official editing experience or state-owned type, challenging a strict separation in which Chosŏn state printing only obstructed nonstate publication.

sources.supports: Examples of Chang Hon's career and elite private use of official type; critique of state/private binary.

counterevidence: These examples do not show unrestricted access to equipment or negate censorship and unequal access.
inference_limits: Underlying studies Walraven (2007) and No (2013) not independently inspected; a few cases cannot measure net institutional effect.

test.mechanism_chain: Official production develops skills/resources -> some actors reuse them privately -> state capacity sometimes complements private publication
test.strongest_rival: A comprehensive state monopoly prevents nonstate production using public skills or equipment.
test.discriminating_observation: Documented private deployment of official expertise or type contradicts the comprehensive form; denied applications would test limits.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S08 supplies counterexamples with references, but the underlying archives were not acquired.
test.remaining_ambiguity: State support and state exclusion can coexist; net effect and who could access resources remain uncertain.

statement: Dittmar identifies 205 adopting cities for 1450–1500; Table I compares them with 1,811 historical cities in its listed polities, selected from places reaching 5,000 residents sometime in 1000–1800.

sources.supports: Adoption-source compilation and denominator definition.

counterevidence: Counts depend on survival and catalogue geography; monasteries and neighbouring centres are handled separately.
inference_limits: Not all European settlements, not a contemporaneous urban census, and not literacy; regression sample sizes differ.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: For European presses in 1450–1500, Dittmar's history connects diffusion to mobile trained printers and entry to financing and sufficiently stable demand; the existence of large cities alone did not determine adoption.

sources.locator: pp. 1153–56; n. 38 on casting uncertainty and n. 40 on equipment valuations
sources.supports: Apprenticeship transmission, financing, customer base and forty of one hundred largest cities without presses in 1500.

counterevidence: The history is partly inherited synthesis; mature casting details are uncertain and demand also shaped location.
inference_limits: No claim that every European press was unregulated, that all operators used identical equipment, or that finance alone explains every nonadopter.

test.mechanism_chain: Trained operators and capital reach a place with customers -> workshop established -> local printing deployment
test.strongest_rival: Demand or city size alone attracts presses; apparent skill networks merely follow profitable locations.
test.discriminating_observation: Large nonadopting cities and adoption varying with technical-network proximity after demand controls; workshop correspondence would be stronger.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S09 records forty of the hundred largest cities without a press and discusses printer mobility, financial requirements and distance.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Demand, skills and funding are jointly selected; historical sequencing and IV assumptions do not fully separate them.
