statement: In Dittmar and Seabold's European printing-city analysis, local competition is associated with lower book prices and changes in publication output; transport costs make location consequential even after technical feasibility.

sources.supports: Book-price evidence, printer entry/death strategy, transport and local market structure.

counterevidence: Competition, customer demand and content can influence one another; death also disrupts expertise and relationships.
inference_limits: Effects conditional on identification assumptions. Prices are from a selected purchasing record; editions are not copies sold or readers.

test.mechanism_chain: Entry or disrupted collusion -> increased local competition -> changed prices and content
test.strongest_rival: Growing demand drives entry and output, or printer death changes scarce expertise directly rather than competition.
test.discriminating_observation: Prices/output shifting with death-induced competitive changes rather than only growing markets; direct skill-channel tests.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S10 compares entries/exits and printer deaths, uses Colón purchase prices and finds lower prices with more local printers; §3 notes different death measures and selection.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Exclusion restriction is substantive; a death can alter more than market structure. This is evidence from the authors' design, not an independent replication.

statement: Studies of early European printing estimate city-growth and content effects using distance from Mainz and printer deaths as instruments; interpretation as causal depends on excluding other geography, expertise and network channels.

sources.locator: §V.E, pp. 1157–63, IV design and comparison with OLS
sources.supports: Distance instrument and tests, outcome is city population growth.
Printer-death designs for competition/content and outcomes.

counterevidence: Pre-trend and control checks support the studies, but exclusion cannot be established by chronology alone; city growth can involve redistribution by migration.
inference_limits: Do not treat city population as national productivity, welfare or a universal print effect. Designs share scholarship and some data foundations.

test.mechanism_chain: Local printing/content access -> useful skills or ideological transmission -> observed city or institutional outcome
test.strongest_rival: Underlying commercial growth or institutions cause both printing and outcomes; geography/deaths affect outcomes through other channels.
test.discriminating_observation: Adoption/output shocks unrelated to pre-trends, sector-specific effects, and falsification of direct channels.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S09 checks prior growth and uses Mainz distance; NET-S10 uses content-specific printer-death variation. Historical production and controls were inspected; estimates not re-estimated.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No independent replication; validity remains conditional and external validity does not extend automatically to other book cultures.

statement: Schwartz finds no inspected original of the alleged Bayezid II/Selim I general printing bans, while the extant 1588 firman protects merchants selling printed Arabic books; a blanket ban is not established evidence.

sources.locator: pp. 6–7, The Non-Extant Firmans and The First Extant Firman; pp. 19–26 on inherited accounts
sources.supports: Documentary contrast and lineage of repeated ban claims.

counterevidence: Absence of these documents does not establish universal permission; narrower restrictions and enforcement could exist.
inference_limits: Claim concerns evidential support for alleged blanket bans, not proof that no Ottoman restrictions ever occurred.

test.mechanism_chain: Proposed general ban -> suppression of printing/trade -> limited uptake
test.strongest_rival: Later writers conflated specific restrictions or preferences into a general ban; permission varied by actor and text.
test.discriminating_observation: An authentic general prohibitory decree or consistent enforcement records versus extant permissions predating 1727.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S11 traces repeated assertions without an original decree and closely reads the 1588 protective firman.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Archival loss remains possible; extant permission defeats a timeless blanket claim but not all narrower prohibitions.

statement: The 1727 grant to Müteferrika permitted particular printing subjects and required learned correctors through the associated fatwa; it both enabled a project and delimited its scope.

sources.locator: pp. 9–11, Ahmed III firman and quoted fatwa
sources.supports: Named permission, subject exclusions and appointment of correctors.

counterevidence: The documents do not state every motive for excluding religious subjects or prove a previous universal prohibition.
inference_limits: Regulatory design establishes permitted scope, not the effectiveness of correction or its impact on sales.

test.mechanism_chain: Petition and expertise claim -> religious/legal approval with correction and subject conditions -> authorised press project
test.strongest_rival: Approval merely formalises an independently viable venture; exclusions reflect broader suppression rather than quality or requested scope.
test.discriminating_observation: Text of the grant/fatwa and actual correcting practices; counterfactual applications denied without conditions.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S11 pp. 9–11 reproduces the permitted subjects and correction condition, and notes the request's own exclusions.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Permit text supports formal enabling/limitation, but cannot identify motives, compliance or marginal commercial effect.

statement: Sabev reports 8,200 initial copies across thirteen editions with known runs, estimates three other runs, and records 2,981 remaining copies in Müteferrika's estate; stock subtraction is not a directly observed sales measure.

sources.supports: Known/assumed runs, estate stock, gifts, different finishing and market exposure.

counterevidence: Large residual stock is consistent with slow sales; earlier titles had more years available and gifts removed copies without sales.
inference_limits: Author's edition grouping and reconstructed figures retained; original register not recounted. No exact profit, sell-through or readership rate.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: Sabev finds Müteferrika prints in sixteen of 335 selected Istanbul askeri probate inventories with more than three books, dated 1724–1748; some owners were religious functionaries.

sources.supports: Selection rules, 335 inventories, sixteen containing prints, religious-functionary owners and stated caveats.

counterevidence: Probates omit living ownership, gifts, donations and readers who borrowed; surviving registers and askeri status select the sample.
inference_limits: High confidence in author's stated result, not independent archive replication. Not a population adoption or literacy denominator.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: In the northern Indian Ocean routes described by fifteenth-/sixteenth-century navigation texts, knowledge of regional and transitional winds mattered within the broad monsoon pattern; season was part of route selection.

sources.supports: Regional wind windows, departure times and route instructions.

counterevidence: Different routes had different windows; general environment does not by itself determine mariners' choices or voyage outcomes.
inference_limits: No fleet-level timing distribution, failure rate or comparison of trained/untrained crews is available.

test.mechanism_chain: Route-specific seasonal knowledge -> chosen departure/bearing -> use of favourable winds and avoidance of hazards
test.strongest_rival: The general monsoon cycle alone suffices; detailed pilot knowledge adds little.
test.discriminating_observation: Instructions distinguishing routes and transitional windows within the same broad season; voyage outcomes would test magnitude.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S13 identifies countervailing winds and an eastward Bay of Bengal window, and reports route-specific dates and hazards.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Detailed prescriptions show relevant distinctions but not actual compliance or a quantified safety benefit.

statement: Staples describes wooden star-altitude aids and magnetic compasses using stellar direction names in late medieval Indian Ocean navigation; Tolmacheva calls magnetic use rare, leaving carriage prevalence unmeasured.

sources.locator: §3 p. 4, fingers, wooden instruments and stellar rhumb names
sources.supports: Layering of standardising instruments and established direction conventions.

sources.locator: paragraph beginning Where the Chinese compass had 28 rhumbs
sources.supports: Stellar compass scheme and assertion of rare magnetic-compass use.

counterevidence: The two sources share underlying texts and differ in emphasis on prevalence; a stellar compass is a directional scheme, not necessarily a magnetic device.
inference_limits: No claim that all ships used compasses, that wooden instruments had a quantified accuracy, or that later kamal descriptions reproduce all earlier instruments.

test.mechanism_chain: Familiar stellar conventions plus measuring aids -> integration with existing navigation skills -> hybrid operating system
test.strongest_rival: An imported magnetic device substitutes for stellar/local knowledge and becomes a universal prerequisite.
test.discriminating_observation: Documents retaining stellar nomenclature and methods alongside devices; actual equipment inventories for prevalence.
test.evidence_sought_found: NET-S13 records integration of stellar names into magnetic directions and wooden measurement; NET-S14 reports rare compass carriage.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Textual prescription is not fleet practice; both scholars rely heavily on the same navigational corpus. Prevalence remains unresolved.

statement: Ibn Majid's surviving instructions include verse suitable for memorisation and lack associated maps, while Portuguese reports describe some Indian Ocean chart use; absence in one corpus does not establish universal chartlessness.

sources.locator: paragraphs beginning It appears that early Portuguese sailors, Curiously, and Moreover
sources.supports: Contrasting chart evidence and verse sailing instructions.
Difference between Arabic literary references and Portuguese testimony; limitations of editions/translations.

counterevidence: Charts may have existed but not survived; verse need not prove every navigator memorised it.
inference_limits: No chart adoption rate or causal effect of oral transmission; inherited corpus is not an exhaustive census of practice.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: The anonymous 1498 voyage narrative reports da Gama seizing a Malindi court servant while demanding pilots, then receiving a pilot and departing with him on 24 April; this documents local expertise and coercion in one crossing episode.

sources.locator: pp. 45–47, Malindi entry for 22 April and Across the Gulf entry for 24 April 1498
sources.supports: Hostage seizure, pilot provision and departure with that pilot.

counterevidence: Narrator's religious identification is unreliable; this single episode does not show the pilot's full role or whether the coercion was necessary.
inference_limits: Do not identify the pilot as Ibn Majid, infer all local recruitment was coerced, or use one voyage as a safety/accuracy comparison.

test.reason: Bounded statement about records, material observations or reported counts; no independent causal effect asserted.

statement: Kyselka’s contemporaneous account records Hōkūleʻa’s 1980 Hawaiʻi–Tahiti return voyage under Nainoa Thompson’s non-instrument navigation, with planetarium training, Mau Piailug’s teaching and escort-based documentation explicitly present.

sources.supports: Training, successful landfall and return, twice-daily position reports and instrument comparison.

counterevidence: This was a supported modern voyage, not a controlled recreation of every ancient condition.
inference_limits: Demonstrates this configuration’s operation; no proof of a particular ancient migration, population uptake or cargo economics.

test.reason: Reports a specific documented voyage and its stated supports, not their separate causal effect.

statement: The 1979–1980 apprenticeship and March 2007 Satawal initiation support an intergenerational, inter-island knowledge-transmission pathway in voyaging renewal; they do not establish that one navigator alone caused a Pacific-wide cultural revival.

sources.supports: Direct learning from Mau and planetarium practice.
Eleven Satawal and five Hawaiʻi initiates and responsibility to perpetuate knowledge.

counterevidence: PVS accounts also celebrate many canoe builders and participants; institution and eyewitness source share a network.
inference_limits: Formal initiation is neither a census of practicing navigators nor a standardized competence test.

test.mechanism_chain: Experienced navigator agrees to teach -> repeated sea and classroom practice -> new navigators operate and receive recognition
test.strongest_rival: Museum science, organizational support and a wider cultural movement independently sustain revival; these may complement teaching
test.discriminating_observation: Training sequence and autonomous voyages by multiple pupils, with explicit instructional histories rather than just shared symbols
test.evidence_sought_found: S01 traces instruction before the 1980 voyage; S03 identifies later pupils and ceremony
test.remaining_ambiguity: No comparison of equally supported trainees without this teaching; many inputs co-varied

statement: PVS records a 1978 capsize and loss of Eddie Aikau, followed by renewed voyages including 1980; revival included severe operational failure, not an uninterrupted sequence of successful demonstrations.

sources.locator: Tragedy and A Generation of Renewal sections
sources.supports: 1978 capsize, rescue/loss, resumption in 1980.

counterevidence: Retrospective narrative emphasizes perseverance.
inference_limits: Does not identify the capsize’s technical cause or quantify safety changes or a voyage failure rate.

test.reason: Bounded chronology of failure and resumption.

statement: Wilson-Hokowhitu’s interviews with women voyagers document ancestral responsibility and identity as expressed reasons for participation, alongside sacrifices of volunteer time; not all interviewees knew or chose to share personal genealogies.

sources.supports: Interview method, participants’ choice about genealogy, volunteering and expressed motivations.

counterevidence: Interview framing explicitly invited genealogical and spiritual reflection.
inference_limits: Purposive qualitative evidence cannot establish prevalence, an exclusive motive, equal entry or wage effects; spiritual accounts are recorded as participants’ interpretations.

test.reason: Direct self-reports about purpose and participation barriers; no causal productivity claim.

statement: At Muldoons Trap Complex, sediment stratigraphy and AMS charcoal dates support an early excavated channel around 6,600 cal BP and a later wall-building episode around 600–800 cal BP, with an intervening hiatus.

sources.supports: Dated fill, mixed horizon, proposed construction sequence.

counterevidence: Fluvial charcoal can be redeposited or have inherited age; investigators explicitly address these problems.
inference_limits: One excavated feature does not date every trap, establish continuous operation, or measure the regional share of food supplied.

test.reason: Summarizes authors’ site-specific chronological interpretation, not a first-invention or continuous-use claim.

statement: Tae Rak’s enlarged drainage works, completed in 1954 despite recorded opposition, sharply curtailed the water conditions for lake-margin trapping; this was institutional and hydrological disabling rather than a demonstrated voluntary choice of a more productive fishery.

sources.supports: Opposition, drainage, short water retention and traps rarely functioning outside floods.
Drain completion in 1954 and later restoration attempts.

counterevidence: Drainage served pastoral flood-control and grazing objectives; those benefits are not evaluated here.
inference_limits: Underlying engineering measurements and original opposition letters not acquired. Sources share project lineage.

test.mechanism_chain: Pastoral drainage authorized over objections -> rapid loss of retained lake water -> trap operating windows shrink
test.strongest_rival: Fishing fell because tastes, labor allocation or alternative livelihoods changed, independently of drainage
test.discriminating_observation: Operation varies with retained water and flood episodes; objections show fishing decline was not simply revealed preference
test.evidence_sought_found: S05 describes rapid recession and flood-only functioning; S06 records failed/restored water-control attempts
test.remaining_ambiguity: No catch time series; labor and ecological change can operate alongside water loss

statement: The 2010 cultural weir restored retained water under a negotiated 52.4 m AHD setting intended to limit flooding of upstream farms; the nomination says this could reactivate most trap complexes but excluded Muldoons at that level.

sources.supports: 2010 restoration, selected water level and differing trap reach.
Failed early trial, planning, hydrological studies, land return and construction.

counterevidence: Restoration also relied on heavy rainfall; the weir was not sufficient by itself.
inference_limits: Not proof that all potentially wetted traps were operated or that precolonial output returned.

test.mechanism_chain: Land return and negotiated engineering -> water retention compatible with neighboring property constraints -> uneven hydraulic reactivation
test.strongest_rival: Rainfall alone restored the lake, with formal restoration incidental
test.discriminating_observation: Retention duration before/after at comparable inflow, and trap elevation relative to negotiated water setting
test.evidence_sought_found: S05 explains selection of level and excluded complex; S06 documents failed trial and successive studies
test.remaining_ambiguity: Matched hydrological time series not acquired; rainfall and gate management interact

statement: Gunditj Mirring reports supported Aboriginal recruitment, training and supervision during January–May 2010 weir construction, including construction and some administrative work.

sources.supports: Government employment support and specific task opportunities.

counterevidence: Implementer account may foreground programme successes.
inference_limits: No employee count, wage, duration beyond construction, retention or distributional impact is reported.

test.reason: Records a specified employment/training programme without inferring household prosperity.

statement: The 2000s Martu studies observe hunting-related burning within a contemporary mixed economy that includes vehicle travel and purchased food; they do not observe an unchanged precolonial regime.

sources.supports: Outstation return, vehicle-supported foraging and stores.
347 sample days, 1,811 bouts and 104 foragers, 2000–2010.

counterevidence: Site use is spatially selective and does not represent all Martu territory.
inference_limits: No estimate of the share of all households practicing burning or its ancient form.

test.reason: Defines actual observed users and configuration.

statement: The 2008 study reports higher mean winter small-game hunting returns with burning than without (656 versus 478 edible kcal/hour), with 152 burning and 89 non-burning hunts; assignment was observational.

sources.supports: Hunt sample sizes, harvest, return-rate and failure comparisons.

counterevidence: Hunters choose when and where to burn; hunting skill and patch condition can differ across groups.
inference_limits: These are foraging-return observations, not wages or a randomized treatment effect.

test.reason: A within-study association with a stated outcome and comparator; no unqualified claim that burning caused the difference.

statement: In the 1999–2010 study region, zones classified as Martu-burning dominated had smaller and more clustered fires and weaker rainfall-related fire-size expansion than lightning-dominated zones; this challenges a climate-only account for these landscapes.

sources.supports: Fire-size and clustering comparison, reported within-regime rainfall associations, proxy regime definition, and burn-age (not ignition-source) ground truth.

counterevidence: Ignitions are proxied by tracks/community distance, and landscape selection is nonrandom. The seasonal fraction burnt did not differ significantly.
inference_limits: No automatic generalization to forests, other Indigenous burning systems, extinction rates or total ecological welfare.

test.mechanism_chain: Hypothesised: repeated small hunting fires -> patches with different fuel ages -> reduced spread under rainfall-driven fuel accumulation; selection into tracked/settled environments remains unresolved.
test.strongest_rival: Climate and substrate alone explain fire patterns; settled/tracked areas occupy different environments
test.discriminating_observation: A direct between-regime interaction contrast would test whether rainfall–fire-size slopes differ. Separating a fuel-mosaic mechanism from environmental selection additionally requires environmental comparability or a defensible causal design; separate significant/nonsignificant slopes establish neither.
test.evidence_sought_found: S08 reports size/clustering and within-regime rainfall associations. Regimes are proxied by community/track distance and fires assigned by centroid; rainfall comes from one station. The 90% ground-truth result checks estimated burn age at 50 points within 500 m of a road/track, not human-versus-lightning ignition classification.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Nonrandom environment, settlement/track selection and ignition proxies remain confounds; no matched intervention or identified between-regime causal slope difference.

statement: The Martu evidence supports a feedback hypothesis in which immediate small-game foraging benefits help maintain repeated burns and landscape heterogeneity without requiring a central planner to direct every ignition.

sources.supports: Task-specific burning benefits and localized landscape response.

sources.locator: Materials and Methods, Martu burning behavior
sources.supports: Gendered task differences, mobility and resulting fire patterns.

counterevidence: Kin obligations, cultural authority and longer-term ecological aims can coexist with immediate benefits; no absence of institutions is claimed.
inference_limits: Does not establish selfish optimization, universal stewardship, or sufficient incentives under new conditions.

test.mechanism_chain: Task-level returns and skilled decisions -> repeated spatially patterned ignitions -> locally maintained mosaic -> further foraging benefits
test.strongest_rival: Burning is maintained principally by norms or intentional collective stewardship; returns correlate with practices but are not decisive
test.discriminating_observation: Task-specific adoption variation, expressed decisions and changes in burning when immediate returns change
test.evidence_sought_found: S07 finds burning concentrated in small-game hunting and no comparable immediate return gain for large-game burning; S08 maps the spatial association
test.remaining_ambiguity: No experiment on motivations or norms; compatible mechanisms remain

statement: Kuk’s published sequence differentiates mounded cultivation around 6,950–6,440 cal BP from ditch cultivation beginning around 4,350–3,980 cal BP; a later account maps multiple, locally varying Phase 3 ditch configurations.

sources.supports: Different phase dates and feature forms.
Phase 3 networks, variable spatial use and earlier possible linear experiments.

counterevidence: Dating boundaries are approximate; only excavated or exposed traces survive.
inference_limits: Not a regional diffusion curve, proof of centralized command or a global independent-invention verdict.

test.reason: Describes a local chronological and material distinction.

statement: Kuk Phase 3 ditches plausibly combined drainage with social functions such as plot marking, while wetland use coexisted with nearby dryland cultivation; the sources cannot separate hydrological, tenure and risk-management drivers.

sources.supports: Wetland/dryland comparison and explicitly alternative social/ecological explanations.

counterevidence: Archaeology records channels more readily than rules, rights, intentions or dryland maintenance.
inference_limits: Contemporary ethnographic analogies do not establish ancient owners, coercion or division of labor.

test.mechanism_chain: Water and/or competing plot claims -> channel digging and maintenance -> drainable and demarcated cultivation spaces
test.strongest_rival: Primarily hydrological adaptation versus primarily territorial demarcation; both predict channels
test.discriminating_observation: Ditch layout versus hydraulic gradient and field boundaries, repair histories, independent tenure/settlement evidence
test.evidence_sought_found: S10 reports hierarchical and nonhierarchical networks and reviews several motivations
test.remaining_ambiguity: Ancient property institutions and labor control remain unknown; functional coexistence does not distinguish primary cause

statement: The Phase 3–4 sequence at Kuk contains a several-hundred-year gap in wetland cultivation, while the reason remains unresolved among hydrological change, dryland alternatives and social disruption; it does not demonstrate disappearance of cultivation knowledge.

sources.supports: Later Phase 3 around 2700–2500 years ago, Phase 4 around 2000 years ago; competing abandonment explanations.

counterevidence: Occupation or gardening beyond the sampled wetland could continue; other valleys have insufficient resolution for simultaneous cessation.
inference_limits: Local discontinuity is not a culture-wide technological loss or regional failure.

test.mechanism_chain: Changed water, alternatives or social access -> wetland maintenance ends -> detectable gap before later ditch configuration
test.strongest_rival: Loss of know-how versus deliberate reallocation or exclusion from workable land
test.discriminating_observation: Synchronous local water rise, changes in dryland crops/settlement, or evidence of population displacement preceding cessation
test.evidence_sought_found: S10 explicitly identifies the alternatives and says the precise reason is unknown
test.remaining_ambiguity: Available chronology does not select a cause; knowledge persistence leaves limited material traces

statement: At M24/11 in northern Te Waipounamu, the 2024 study associates probable kūmara starch and other proposed crop remains with fourteenth-century cultivation contexts and identifies later kūmara remains after 1650.

sources.supports: Context-specific microbotany, short-life dates and later deposits.

counterevidence: Taxonomic identification relies on morphology and context; crop-abundance inference is not directly proportional to surviving starch counts.
inference_limits: No continent-wide arrival date, harvest quantity, uninterrupted cultivation or universal disappearance of other crops.

test.reason: Reports bounded site evidence and authors’ probabilistic taxonomic interpretations.

statement: The Cook Strait experimental gardens demonstrate feasible growth of selected Māori kūmara cultivars under 1999–2002 conditions, but modern plant treatment, fencing, windbreaks, unreplicated plots and nontraditional storage prevent treating their yields as ancient farm performance.

sources.supports: Trial design, returned/tissue-cultured collection, results, storage caveat and limits.

counterevidence: The experiments were explicitly exploratory and iwi authorities were consulted; these limits do not make practical growth results worthless.
inference_limits: Per-hectare extrapolation from tiny plots is not measured ancient output, adoption or labor productivity.

test.reason: Separates an observed feasibility demonstration from historical adoption and causal comparison.

statement: At Pōhatu, the 2025 collaborative study used Mana Whenua knowledge to guide questions and interpret modified soils; weak support for initially considered marine fertilizers led to further testing of terrestrial plant inputs, with kānuka a plausible rather than certain source.

sources.supports: Research sequence, knowledge-guided interpretation, gravel additions and fertilizer alternatives.

counterevidence: Geochemical signatures are not unique; only two profiles and selected candidate amendments were examined.
inference_limits: Knowledge systems contribute different evidence and meanings; agreement is not blanket authentication of all historical details.

test.mechanism_chain: Place-linked knowledge and shared questions -> targeted soil sampling and interpretation -> candidate amendments revised through joint discussion -> bounded reconstruction
test.strongest_rival: Soil chemistry alone would yield the same conclusions, or any favored tradition could be fitted after the fact
test.discriminating_observation: Documented sequence in which an initial candidate fails, further candidates are proposed, and tests discriminate rather than merely affirm
test.evidence_sought_found: S12 section4.3 describes marine hypotheses failing Mn matching and expanded plant testing; sections1–3 document prior collaboration
test.remaining_ambiguity: No parallel research team without community input; exact ancient fertilizer and timing remain uncertain

statement: Pōhatu’s contemporary investigation is framed by Mana Whenua as recovery of place-based cultivation knowledge after land alienation and disconnection; the published study supports reconnection and food-sovereignty aspirations but does not measure restored horticultural adoption.

sources.supports: Private ownership over 150 years, displacement narrative, research questions and intended restoration.

counterevidence: Historical land-transfer details rely partly on cited scholarship and community history, not a deed audit in this contribution.
inference_limits: Do not convert an aspiration or research partnership into a completed livelihood transition.

test.reason: Distinguishes documented research purpose and historical account from unmeasured deployment outcomes.

statement: The Martu study describes customary rights to burn, possible retribution for burning others’ areas, and social value attached to care for Country; localized burning was not institution-free individual optimization.

sources.locator: Materials and Methods, paragraphs on social/economic disincentives and kanyinin/Jukurrpa
sources.supports: Ethnographic account of rights, costs, responsibilities and public-good recognition.

counterevidence: Norms and sanctions are described by researchers, not quantified as an independent enforcement dataset.
inference_limits: No claim that all Martu follow identical rules, that enforcement is equal, or that social incentives alone determine fire outcomes.

test.reason: Records the published ethnographic account of governance and meanings without assigning isolated causal weights.

statement: Enomoto reports 436 hunting firearms among 955 Shiiba-mountain households in 1745 and 586 firearms in 1836; these are local recorded stocks, not a national ownership rate.

sources.supports: Counts inherited from Fujiki, Katanagari, pp. 168–169.

counterevidence: Household denominator for 1836 is not supplied; recorded ownership may exclude unlicensed guns.
inference_limits: Original village registers not inspected; neither persons armed nor annual use can be calculated.

test.reason: Bounded description of a published local example.

statement: Legal crop-protection and hunting use, together with recorded commoner ownership, contradicts a general account of Tokugawa Japan eliminating guns.

sources.supports: Local firearm records and distinctions among possession, carriage and use.
Common rural firearms and farm-tool uses.
Continued elite and non-elite peacetime niches.

counterevidence: Restrictions and confiscations occurred; persistence does not imply unchanged military effectiveness or unconstrained ownership.
inference_limits: Sources share Japanese historical scholarship; high confidence applies to rejecting total elimination, not to national abundance.

test.reason: Tests a categorical absence claim using positive local evidence; no causal estimate of regulation.

statement: Task-specific permission and peacetime elite appropriation helped accommodate continued firearm use within Tokugawa hierarchies, rather than requiring universal rejection of the technology.

sources.supports: Differentiated regulation and village use.
Licensed commoner use and elite marksmanship/status.

counterevidence: Enforcement weakness or unofficial circulation could also sustain guns; no estimate of their relative weight.
inference_limits: This is a scoped accommodation mechanism, not proof that peace or hierarchy caused a national innovation slowdown.

test.mechanism_chain: Crop/hunting needs and elite interests -> authorities authorize differentiated uses -> firearms retain legitimate niches -> persistence under regulation.
test.strongest_rival: Persistence merely reflects inability to enforce a universal ban.
test.discriminating_observation: Officially acknowledged permissible uses and elite use, not only illicit caches.
test.evidence_sought_found: S01 records authorized local possession; S03 summarizes regulated farming and elite marksmanship.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No matched-domain enforcement comparison; peace, status and livelihood incentives co-evolve.

statement: Howell interprets a shift in Edo-hinterland gun meanings from farm implements toward weapons in the 1840s as responding to anxiety about rural disorder.

sources.supports: Author states the 1840s change and disorder interpretation.

counterevidence: The study might also reflect changing enforcement, reporting vocabulary or later military developments.
inference_limits: Abstract-only access; no independently inspected beliefs, petitions or individual trajectory.

test.mechanism_chain: Perceived disorder -> villagers reinterpret guns as defensive weapons -> social use/meaning changes.
test.strongest_rival: A change in record language or administrative classification rather than in actual behavior.
test.discriminating_observation: Contemporaneous petitions and firing/use records showing changes before external military rearmament.
test.evidence_sought_found: S02 abstract gives the interpretation; underlying examples were unavailable.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cannot separate behavior, rhetoric and selection from the abstract.

statement: Guan, Palma and Wu distinguish full silver convertibility (1260–76), nominal convertibility (1277–1309) and a fiat regime from 1310; exchange availability and official status were distinct.

sources.supports: Authors reconstruct regime stages and spatially unequal redemption access.

counterevidence: Exact transition boundaries vary by one year in parts of manuscript; local availability could diverge from legal promise.
inference_limits: Periodization is historians’ reconstruction; no uniform household access is inferred.

test.reason: Description of reconstructed monetary configurations.

statement: The study’s reconstructed respectability CPI estimates annual inflation of 11.0% for 1260–1290, 1.8% for 1290–1340 and 4.5% for 1340–1355, contradicting uniform century-long hyperinflation.

sources.supports: Price basket, sparse observations, interpolation, and reported compound rates.

counterevidence: Individual prices and regions differed; the final collapse extends beyond 1355 price data.
inference_limits: About a dozen observations per commodity with interpolation/extrapolation; modelled index, not modern continuous official CPI. No household cost-of-living equivalence.

test.reason: Reports the authors’ bounded calculation and its measurement method.

statement: In the reconstructed 1260–1355 series, civil-war frequency correlates with greater nominal and real note issuance; imperial grants do not show comparable statistical associations in Table 4.

sources.supports: Civil-war coefficients and distinctions among nominal/real issues and rival demands.

counterevidence: Natural disasters weakly correlate with real issuance at the 10% level; external-war coefficients are not significant.
inference_limits: Political disorder, inflation and fiscal erosion can reinforce each other. No exogenous shock identifies the fiscal channel; absence of significance is not proof of no effect.

test.mechanism_chain: Civil conflict -> fiscal demands/tax difficulty -> greater note issuance -> potential pressure on currency value.
test.strongest_rival: Inflation and collapsing revenue cause civil conflict; or imperial grants/disasters dominate spending.
test.discriminating_observation: Different associations for war types and grants, with temporally ordered independently measured fiscal shortages.
test.evidence_sought_found: S04 Table 4 finds civil-war associations in nominal/real issues, no grant association, and weak real-disaster associations; only sparse fiscal totals.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Annual reconstructed time series does not remove reciprocal causation or omitted political changes; fiscal intermediate evidence incomplete.

statement: Yuan legal monetary unification coexisted with regional and task-specific practices: Ichimaru reports different uses of guanwen and dingliang, while Guan et al. report silver property transactions despite official restrictions.

sources.supports: Regional account-unit and government/commercial distinctions.
Private silver use and Yunnan cowry exception.

counterevidence: A regional unit of account is not automatically a different circulating medium.
inference_limits: Contract-level evidence in S05 not inspected; formal legal-tender scope must not be equated with every transaction.

test.reason: Separates observable institutional rules, units of account and reported practices.

statement: Polo’s paper-money narrative combines threat of punishment for refusal with portability, official authentication and damaged-note replacement; it cannot independently establish willing universal acceptance.

sources.supports: Narrative explicitly juxtaposes coercion and convenient transactions/redemption.

counterevidence: The narrative also insists on ready acceptance and enormous imperial riches; these are claims to assess, not measured outcomes.
inference_limits: Confidence is high about text content; the frequency of punishments, distribution of consent and national coverage are unknown.

test.reason: Source-critical description, not validation of every traveler assertion.

statement: Late-Qing telegraph development included strategic state priorities and controlled private operation; the Gao–Lei sample records office access for 64 of 130 rice-reporting prefectures by 1904.

sources.locator: pp. 7–9 and 12–13, sections I.A and II.B
sources.supports: Strategic line-building narrative; explicit sample treatment counts.

counterevidence: Routes could still reflect economic geography; state priorities do not prove random placement.
inference_limits: Sample is nine provinces, not all Qing territory; office presence does not measure affordability, uptime or individual usage.

test.reason: Bounded deployment description and denominator.

statement: Yoon argues that shareholder-dividend priorities, underinvestment, high charges and technical/service problems limited the telegraph’s popular use even after network establishment.

sources.supports: Author links shareholder returns, equipment choices, pricing and limited market reach.

counterevidence: Gao–Lei find price effects consistent with commercially useful communication; limited mass use is compatible with gains among traders.
inference_limits: Abstract-only; no audited tariff-demand series or proof that dividends, rather than scarce capital/risk, caused underinvestment.

test.mechanism_chain: Dividend demands -> constrained equipment investment/high fees -> unreliable expensive service -> restricted public uptake.
test.strongest_rival: High capital costs, risk or low demand require high tariffs; technical failures precede rather than result from financing choices.
test.discriminating_observation: Investment decisions and dividend commitments preceding delays, with comparable capital-cost routes or customer elasticities.
test.evidence_sought_found: S08 abstract supplies mechanism; full budgets and customer series unavailable. S07 finds beneficial price effects on a different margin.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cannot choose among financing and demand mechanisms; do not generalize to all state/private ownership models.

statement: Zhou and Ding portray Sheng Xuanhuai as defending telegraph investors against court encroachment while also having entangled personal interests; the abstract records a proposal for state purchase instead of appropriation.

sources.supports: Conflicted official/investor interests and purchase-versus-confiscation proposal.

counterevidence: The Chinese abstract also notes Sheng sometimes pressured shareholders from the court’s side.
inference_limits: A proposal is not completed reform, public consultation or popular legitimacy; underlying correspondence not inspected.

test.reason: Attributed description of actors and proposals, not a causal claim of modernization.

statement: Gao and Lei’s difference-in-differences study estimates that telegraph office access reduced monthly maximum high-quality rice prices by about 4.2–5.5% of the sample mean in 130 prefectures over 1870–1904.

sources.supports: Data, specifications, effect magnitudes and pretrend checks.

counterevidence: Office placement was not randomized; reporting changes and time-varying conflicts could remain. Lower-quality rice estimates are smaller/less precise.
inference_limits: Outcome is reported monthly wholesale maxima, not average consumer expenditure, famine deaths or welfare; original regressions not replicated.

test.mechanism_chain: Faster information across existing trade routes -> merchants adjust orders -> lower local price extremes.
test.strongest_rival: Coincident transport/institutional change, placement selection or altered reporting accounts for falling maxima.
test.discriminating_observation: Pretrends, transport/port controls, route/subsample tests and reactions to connected versus unconnected external shocks.
test.evidence_sought_found: S07 checks pretrends, railway/treaty-port controls, excludes selected locations and tests weather/network channels.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Assumed June treatment month, spillovers, official reporting quality and staggered-treatment assumptions remain; no household outcomes.

statement: The same study finds telegraph access dampened local-weather price effects but increased sensitivity to weather in connected regions; price volatility rose in previously stable markets and fell in previously volatile ones.

sources.supports: Weather-location interactions, disconnected-region placebo and volatility heterogeneity.

counterevidence: The result is shared-risk transmission, not uniform stabilization; estimated mechanisms depend on exposure weights and reported weather.
inference_limits: Same sample as K13, not independent corroboration; no distribution of gains among net buyers, sellers or laborers.

test.mechanism_chain: Connected price information -> trade arbitrage links markets -> local shocks spread -> less local isolation and redistributed risk.
test.strongest_rival: General administrative change reduces price volatility everywhere regardless of network.
test.discriminating_observation: Opposite responses to local and connected distant shocks; no similar response to disconnected shocks.
test.evidence_sought_found: S07 reports these directional tests and heterogeneous volatility by baseline risk.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Trade flows and household welfare not directly measured; weight/model choices and common reporting may matter.

statement: The 1812 imperial decree retained metric base units while ordering commercially familiar fractions/multiples and dual markings on instruments, and retained official metric teaching.

sources.supports: Direct decree on unchanged units, adapted instruments and teaching.
Retail implementation and legal continuity.

counterevidence: The resulting arrangements modified decimal practice; describing unchanged base units alone would hide a substantial compromise.
inference_limits: Law states what was authorized and intended, not how widely instruments were supplied or accepted.

test.reason: Direct legal configuration, carefully distinguished from compliance.

statement: A material implementation gap accompanied early metric mandates: Treat reports that secondary standards had not been distributed when compulsory use was declared in 1795.

sources.supports: Secondary standards/commercial instrument shortfall.
Municipal standard provision and later conversion tables.

counterevidence: Familiarity, pricing interests and political disruption also constrained uptake; instruments alone would not ensure adoption.
inference_limits: Retrospective evidence does not estimate what share of delay was caused by supply constraints.

test.mechanism_chain: Mandate before local standards/instruments -> users lack calibrated practical implements -> legal uniformity fails to ensure comparable practice.
test.strongest_rival: Users had sufficient implements but deliberately resisted new measures.
test.discriminating_observation: Dated deliveries/orders compared with local compliance, including places supplied early.
test.evidence_sought_found: S13 states missing secondary standards; S12 describes municipal supply and tables. No matched delivery/compliance panel inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Physical and social obstacles could operate together; relative contributions unmeasured.

statement: The law of 4 July 1837 repealed the 1812 arrangement and prohibited nonmetric measures from 1 January 1840; this supplies a legal deadline, not a date of universal practical adoption.

sources.supports: Repeal and effective date.
Translated prohibitions including commercial/legal settings.

counterevidence: Older words and task measures persisted according to the Isère synthesis.
inference_limits: Both accounts derive from the same law; original Bulletin des lois not inspected. No national compliance denominator.

test.reason: Corroborated legal sequence; explicit non-equivalence to use.

statement: The Isère archival synthesis describes customary measures tied to agricultural work and continued rural usage beyond the 1840 legal deadline; practical task fit is a plausible part of persistence, not a measured universal preference.

sources.locator: PDF pp. 2, 6–9, especially journal/land-work discussion and long-run coda
sources.supports: Task-linked area measures, local implementation and later coexistence.

counterevidence: Habit, limited schooling, fraud and political resistance may also explain use; the source does not isolate these channels.
inference_limits: Coda extends beyond 1795–1840 and is used only to reject instantaneous displacement. Neither continued terminology nor local examples establish unchanged quantities nationally.

test.mechanism_chain: Established work/commodity conventions -> customary units remain useful for local tasks -> continued mixed practice despite a legal standard.
test.strongest_rival: Pure inertia or educational exclusion, with no continuing practical utility.
test.discriminating_observation: Contexts where a task-linked measure persists as the task persists and changes when work changes, despite ability to use metric units.
test.evidence_sought_found: S12 links the journal to horse-ploughing and describes later rural coexistence; no individual longitudinal literacy/use evidence.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Source offers qualitative association, not a discriminating controlled comparison.

statement: In Busia’s research-assisted on-farm trials, half-teaspoon CAN top-dressing produced a mean calculated seasonal return of 36%, while the full Ministry-recommended fertilizer/hybrid-seed package had a negative mean return; higher physical yield did not make every input configuration profitable.

sources.supports: Randomised adjacent plots, dose-specific yield and calculated return comparisons.

counterevidence: Small plots, assisted application and noisy seasonal returns; risk and labour assumptions affect interpretation.
inference_limits: Identifies tested plot-package performance under those conditions, not farm-wide realised profits or a profitable dose for every farmer.

test.mechanism_chain: Specified dose/package -> changed input application -> yield less input cost -> calculated return
test.strongest_rival: All fertilizer packages have uniformly high private returns, versus configuration-specific economics.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare net returns, not only yields, across randomised doses/packages.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S02 Table1: positive mean return at half teaspoon; negative at one teaspoon and full official package.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Labour/assistance, small-plot noise and heterogeneous future conditions limit economic transportability.

statement: Randomised harvest-time SAFI offers increased household fertilizer use in treated seasons (adjusted +14.3pp and +18.1pp in the two main seasons), but did not produce a detectable persistent increase after the offer ceased.

sources.supports: Season-specific randomised offer effects and follow-up coefficients.

counterevidence: About one-quarter of originally sampled farmers lacked adoption data; full-control denominators smaller. Persistent effects could be smaller than study precision.
inference_limits: Household any-plot use, not stable individual habit, market-wide diffusion or sustained welfare gain.

test.mechanism_chain: Early delivered purchase offer -> additional acquisition/use this season -> possible learning/wealth change -> later use
test.strongest_rival: One use permanently changes knowledge, wealth or habit enough to maintain increased adoption.
test.discriminating_observation: Positive later-season effects when original offer is absent.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S01 Table4 shows treatment-season gains and later estimates near comparison-group usage.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No detectable persistence does not prove no learning; liquidity, shocks or small scale may offset learned benefits.

statement: SAFI’s pattern is consistent with procrastination/commitment mechanisms, but does not uniquely identify present bias: late free delivery estimated +9–10pp without significance, the early–late difference had p=.08, and timing-choice take-up did not fully match the simple model.

sources.supports: Timing arms, prechoice, maize-purchase test, pilot intention/purchase gaps and alternative explanations.

counterevidence: Seasonal liquidity, opportunity costs, trusted delivery and a surprise late offer can also matter; pilots use purchases rather than subsequent use.
inference_limits: No independently elicited present-bias parameter. Cannot equate one insignificant arm with zero or read welfare rankings directly from trial outcomes.

test.mechanism_chain: Harvest-time small acquisition-cost reduction -> earlier purchase/less delay -> more seasonal use
test.strongest_rival: Time-consistent farmers with seasonal resources, fixed costs and changing opportunities also prefer early offers.
test.discriminating_observation: Announce late offers in advance; vary liquidity independently; directly elicit intertemporal choices and relate them prospectively to response.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S01 includes timing prechoice, favourable maize-purchase test and smaller announced-delay pilots; these constrain some simple rivals, but p=.08 timing contrast and model misfit remain.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Several timing and saving motives share predictions; favourable maize sale is not a complete liquidity intervention.

statement: Among 489 surveyed Indonesian seaweed growers, 86% could not state their current pod size and 87% could not state an optimal size, whereas most could state spacing; these beliefs were elicited before uptake outcomes and alongside observed farm practices.

sources.supports: Input-specific knowledge responses and independently recorded plot practices.

counterevidence: Being unable to answer in grams may partly reflect measurement language rather than complete lack of practical knowledge.
inference_limits: A bounded descriptive contrast, not a universal cognitive deficit among farmers.

test.reason: Reports baseline answers and the measurement design without assigning a psychological cause.

statement: In the seaweed trial, input changes were more evident after personalised summaries than after trial participation alone; measured pod-size phase differences were significant, but the approximately 7g post-summary treatment effect itself was imprecise.

sources.supports: Post-summary self-reported change +0.162/+0.171; pod-size effects 6.951/7.316g; phase-difference p=.003/.015; fixed-effect post-summary p=.14.

counterevidence: Self-reported phase-difference equality not rejected (p=.148/.221); spacing did not change. All treated farmers received summary later, rather than randomising explanation time separately.
inference_limits: Randomised trial-package versus control supports effects of exposure path, not a pure independently randomised summary-only effect or long-run income improvement.

test.mechanism_chain: On-plot trial plus later interpreted results -> information usable for input choice -> subsequent pod-size/practice changes
test.strongest_rival: Experience alone eventually causes learning; later change need not arise specifically from noticing.
test.discriminating_observation: Separate trial-only, delayed-learning and summary-only arms at the same follow-up date, with objective practices.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S03 TableIV provides randomised treated/control contrasts at two stages and objective weights; phase differences for weights support a change after summaries.
test.remaining_ambiguity: No independent summary timing randomisation; direct effect precision is weak and farmer demand effects possible.

statement: Limited attention is a plausible account of the seaweed input-specific pattern, but explanation also reduces computational demands and can alter credibility; the evidence does not isolate attention as the sole mechanism.

sources.supports: Authors consider labour costs, numeracy and perceptibility; farmers knew a summary was coming.

counterevidence: Baseline differences across input dimensions support attention; however, spacing and weight tasks need not impose the same calculation burden.
inference_limits: No laboratory findings borrowed from cited papers; neither an innate deficit nor irrationality established. The model itself allows costly attention to be chosen optimally given mistaken priors.

test.mechanism_chain: Unnoticed input dimension -> raw experience not encoded -> salient explanation -> changed practice
test.strongest_rival: Summary makes arithmetic easier, provides trusted advice or simply arrives after enough time.
test.discriminating_observation: Vary salience while holding calculations, recommendation and timing fixed; independently measure attention/recall.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S03 baseline knowledge plus measurements fits attention; §IV.C explicitly discusses computational rival and footnote29 notes anticipated summaries.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Belief reports are stronger than inference from uptake alone but not direct attention measurement.

statement: In the 120-village Malawi extension experiment, performance incentives to ordinary peer communicators increased their experimentation/communication and downstream adoption; simply appointing local communicators without incentives did not reliably produce that diffusion.

sources.supports: Cross-randomised communicator/incentive design, knowledge exams and observed practices.

counterevidence: Peer strategy used five communicators versus one lead farmer; number, relevance and identity not separately randomised. Incentives can signal priorities as well as pay for effort.
inference_limits: Supports incentive-dependent communication in this institutional programme, not a universal claim that peers need payment or that ordinary identity alone causes adoption.

test.mechanism_chain: Performance reward -> communicator effort/own demonstration -> recipient knowledge -> farm adoption
test.strongest_rival: Passive diffusion follows automatically from selecting respected/local farmers, without effort incentives.
test.discriminating_observation: Cross-randomise rewards; observe communicator actions and recipient knowledge/practices rather than correlate friends’ uptake.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S05 documents weak unincentivised effects and stronger rewarded peer communication/adoption.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Payment, task salience, number of contacts and demonstrator adoption interact; identity-versus-number remains unresolved.

statement: In the separate 200-village Malawi network experiment, central-seed targeting increased pit-planting diffusion relative to extension-worker selection; adoption-rate differences were significant in year two but not year three, and 45% of benchmark villages had no non-seed adopter after three years.

sources.supports: Same two seed slots across four selection arms; diffusion rates and any-non-seed village outcome.

counterevidence: Some benchmark villages did diffuse; most farmers still did not adopt even under central targeting. Network collection expensive; CRM differs from pit planting.
inference_limits: No necessity edge warranted. The larger village-level probability of any adoption and average individual uptake are different estimands.

test.mechanism_chain: Network-based choice of two trained seeds -> wider relevant contacts -> some non-seed adoption
test.strongest_rival: Any two locally selected informed farmers eventually yield equivalent reach over observed time.
test.discriminating_observation: Hold training/seed count fixed and randomise selection rule; compare both average adoption and stalls.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S04 reports ~3pp rate advantage in years2/3, precise only year2, and fewer no-diffusion villages under central targeting.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Three years cannot establish permanent stalls; centrality co-varies with other seed attributes.

statement: Female-reserved communicator roles in the Malawi 143-village study elicited lower recipient ratings and lower training attendance despite comparable measured communicator knowledge/use; pooled downstream knowledge/adoption and yields did not show a precise corresponding gender penalty.

sources.supports: Objective competence, recipient ratings, training attendance, knowledge/adoption/yields measured separately.

counterevidence: Some female-recipient knowledge/adoption contrasts are negative at p<.10; pooled imprecision is not equivalence. Unreserved roles not exclusively male by design.
inference_limits: Identifies effects of reservation arrangements, not a biological sex effect or complete causal mediation through prejudice.

test.mechanism_chain: Reservation changes messenger composition -> recipient appraisal/contact -> possible learning/adoption change
test.strongest_rival: Lower reception simply reflects lower measured technical competence or necessarily creates lower final diffusion.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare objective communicator competence, independent recipient perceptions and downstream results within assignment arms.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S06 finds no measured learning gap, lower attendance/ratings, but weak pooled downstream penalties.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Selected communicators may differ on unmeasured teaching qualities; perception elicitation after assignment and heterogeneous subgroup results limit mediation claims.

statement: The Malawi network data support a multiple-contact learning interpretation, but complex contagion is not uniquely established: connectedness can change exposure, demonstration and persuasion as well as reinforcement of beliefs.

sources.locator: §5 and pp.5–6; individual two-seed link analysis
sources.supports: Two-seed connections predict learning/adoption under randomised seed assignments; author explicitly notes alternatives.

counterevidence: Larger effects where baseline knowledge low and land more suitable are consistent with learning; neither is exclusive to a threshold mechanism.
inference_limits: Do not turn network topology into a universal psychological threshold or infer that one contact never suffices.

test.mechanism_chain: Multiple informed connections -> reinforced useful information -> learning/adoption
test.strongest_rival: More contacts increase encounter probability, effort or demonstrator relevance without a discrete reinforcement threshold.
test.discriminating_observation: Hold contact time/content and seed effort constant while varying independent sources; measure belief updating before use.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S04 uses assignment-induced two-seed exposure and knowledge; PSY-S05 demonstrates that communication effort itself can respond to incentives.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Cross-study comparison suggests a rival rather than jointly identifying a mechanism; studies share institutions and researchers.

statement: In Humes et al.’s 154-completer trial, both effective audiology-fitted and consumer-selected preset aids improved major hearing-benefit measures versus placebo, while satisfaction and preliminary keep intention differed and daily logged use did not differ significantly across service arms.

sources.locator: Results, Figures6–10; Table5; preliminary decision-to-keep section
sources.supports: Randomised service comparisons with several distinct outcomes; 81% versus55% versus36% preliminary keep intention.
CST test was at +1dB SNR, not originally reported +3dB.

counterevidence: Selected volunteers, short period, no prior use and same hardware; absence of significance is not proof identical efficacy. Speech-test calibration corrected.
inference_limits: The intention percentages are not actual final retention rates. Consumer model simulated OTC access within a clinic; does not verify all OTC products or user groups.

test.mechanism_chain: Effective amplification plus specified delivery -> task benefit -> satisfaction/use/retention decisions
test.strongest_rival: Professional contact/placebo alone accounts for apparent hearing gains, or usage alone measures all benefit.
test.discriminating_observation: Same hardware with placebo programming and blinded outcome assessment; separate benefit, hours and choice.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S07 active models beat placebo on benefit, but usage fails to separate groups; S13 corrects test calibration.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Fitting, orientation and interpersonal service bundled; post-trial rescue fitting not independently randomised.

statement: The hearing-aid price comparison was not randomised: earlier participants paid $3,600 and later participants $600; the null price findings for many benefit measures and concentration of returns at the high price cannot identify a causal price effect.

sources.locator: Introduction final paragraphs; Methods Trial Design; final returns section
sources.supports: Sequential cohorts; 17/20 returners paid high price, versus60/134 keepers.

counterevidence: Price cohorts were roughly balanced across service arms, but that does not randomise price or remove recruitment/time confounding.
inference_limits: Neither price irrelevance nor a quantified affordability effect inferred.

test.reason: Methodological fact and observed cohort association; deliberately no causal claim about price.

statement: In Wallhagen’s 91 Bay Area help-seeking dyads, independently elicited accounts linked visible hearing aids with age, disability and perceived competence; some participants rejected or discounted stigma, especially in supportive relationships.

sources.locator: Methods; Results: altered self-perception, ageism/vanity and supportive/nonsupportive others
sources.supports: Separate repeated interviews elicited meanings and reasons before/after choices, including contrary accounts.

counterevidence: Self-reports may rationalise decisions, and stigma can coexist with costs and poor benefit. Participants already seeking assessment; predominantly White.
inference_limits: Evidence establishes heterogeneous expressed meanings, not universal innate preferences, a stigma prevalence estimate or a causal effect of de-stigmatisation.

test.mechanism_chain: Social meanings of visible aids -> anticipated social response/identity cost -> help-seeking or use decision
test.strongest_rival: Low experienced benefit/cost explains refusal, and identity narratives are post-hoc rationalisation.
test.discriminating_observation: Measure concerns before decisions and manipulate social framing/support while holding device benefit/access fixed.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S09 uses repeated separate interviews and follows decisions, including supportive and unconcerned participants; no framing experiment.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Narratives establish a plausible local mechanism but cannot estimate mediation or independently establish actual discrimination.

statement: In a separate earlier Indiana volunteer cohort, 105 of 139 analysed never-users purchased hearing aids and 21 purchasers returned them; returners had poorer measured aided outcomes, while nonpurchasers differed mainly in perceived difficulties and expectations.

sources.locator: Methods Participants; Abstract; Results adherent/nonadherent and keep/return comparisons
sources.supports: Analytic sample and outcome associations after controlling for hearing severity.

counterevidence: Only34 nonpurchasers returned for measurement; only 15 of 21 returners completed end-of-trial outcomes. Unmeasured confounding and selective participation.
inference_limits: These are research-volunteer analytic denominators, not population adoption/abandonment rates. No claim that beliefs cause purchase or poor benefit alone causes return.

test.reason: Original observational associations and counts; separate stages of adoption without a causal preference inference.

statement: For Bihar’s bicycle-grant exposure, the adjusted triple-difference estimate was +5.2pp in age-appropriate grade-9 enrolment/completion for girls, relative to older cohorts, boys and Jharkhand; it is not an estimate of actual cycling or total lifetime secondary enrolment.

sources.supports: Age14–15 versus16–17; female/male; Bihar/Jharkhand; full-controls N=30,112, coefficient0.052(SE0.025).

counterevidence: Estimate falls from0.103 without controls to0.052 with household controls; no randomised rollout. Concurrent state reforms remain a concern.
inference_limits: Causal interpretation conditional on difference-in-differences assumptions and age/cohort comparability.

test.mechanism_chain: Earmarked grant -> more feasible school access -> age-appropriate grade9 participation
test.strongest_rival: General Bihar reform or household/cohort composition would create similar measured change without bicycles.
test.discriminating_observation: Check gender/state/cohort pretrends, socioeconomic controls and ineligible-grade placebo.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S10 Tables1/2/8: triple-difference pretrend not rejected; grade8 placebo near zero; adjustment materially reduces estimate.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Tests cannot exclude all cohort-specific female reforms or ascertain individual bicycle use.

statement: Bihar’s distance heterogeneity and ineligible-grade placebo favour a school-access channel, but do not separate saved travel time, safety, peer travel and changed social norms.

sources.locator: Distance analysis §§II–III; Table8 pp.343–345; discussion pp.346–348
sources.supports: Effects concentrated farther from secondary schools; grade8 placebo0.001; norms/safety discussed as possible channels.

counterevidence: Roads and law/order may complement bicycles even if they do not explain the whole effect; outcomes do not directly measure household norms.
inference_limits: Do not call Bihar a randomised norm-change intervention or treat enrolment as evidence of unrestricted mobility.

test.mechanism_chain: Grant-enabled riding -> lower distance/safety burden -> participation and possible peer/norm feedback
test.strongest_rival: Other reforms or a conditional transfer’s income/incentive effect generate enrolment without norm change.
test.discriminating_observation: Compare distances and noneligible grades; separately measure commute, danger and norms; randomise mobility versus unrestricted cash.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S10 distance gradient and grade8 placebo support access; no direct isolation of safety/norms or cash-only counterfactual.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Several pathways predict the same distance pattern; equilibrium social spillovers not independently identified.

statement: A later Bihar reanalysis finds stronger bicycle-programme estimates in villages with all-weather road connectivity, but its health-facility road proxy and nonrandom infrastructure do not establish that such roads are strictly necessary.

sources.supports: DLHS health-facility access proxy, quadruple-difference estimates and authors’ unobserved-difference caution.

counterevidence: No-road indicator permits dry-season tracks; unobserved village differences and route quality remain. Same main survey/policy lineage as S10.
inference_limits: Contributory infrastructure hypothesis, not independent replication or bounded technical necessity.

test.mechanism_chain: Usable roads plus bicycle access -> reliable travel -> school participation
test.strongest_rival: Road variable proxies wealth, governance, school access or treatment implementation rather than causal complementarity.
test.discriminating_observation: Actual school-route quality and exogenous road changes interacted with bicycle offers.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S12 uses health-facility road connectivity, controls and pretrend checks, finding heterogeneity; cannot observe precise school routes.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Insignificant disconnected estimate cannot distinguish absence from imprecision; no factorial road experiment.

statement: In Zambia’s 100-school experiment, the bicycle-plus-support package reduced self-reported one-way commute by 35.08 minutes (control 103.77) and last-week absence by 0.29 days (control 1.01) at one year; the final article abstract rounds these to 34% and 29%.

sources.supports: 25 payment,20 free,55 control schools; commute N=1,879; absence N=1,952; school-clustered randomisation inference.
Rounded34% commute and29% absenteeism reductions; final full text not acquired.

counterevidence: Differential follow-up and self-report; programme includes mechanics, committees and use restrictions. One-year dropout/grade-transition/English effects not significant.
inference_limits: Effect of the installed package on eligible already-enrolled girls; not a bare-asset effect, school-entry effect or proof all girls can use bicycles.

test.mechanism_chain: Bike/support offer -> usable school transport -> shorter commute -> better attendance
test.strongest_rival: Common schooling improvement explains gains, or mere stated enthusiasm without travel/task change.
test.discriminating_observation: Randomised school control and concrete travel/attendance outcomes, with attrition checks and longer administrative follow-up.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S11 Tables1/4 show large specific effects; S14 abstract confirms rounded direction/magnitude; manuscript attrition bounds inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Self-report not blinded; no independent randomisation of maintenance/custody; follow-up excludes some girls and later records are separately scoped.

statement: Zambia’s nominal-fee versus free bicycle arms did not yield precise differences in first-stage transport or reported empowerment outcomes; a parental-payment/psychological-ownership explanation is therefore not identified by one arm being significant and the other not.

sources.supports: Formal fee/free equality p-values: commute .40; aggregate empowerment .13; agency subscales .11–.99.

counterevidence: Some fee-arm point estimates higher; trial is not a powered equivalence/noninferiority design, and nearly universal uptake limits selection tests.
inference_limits: No general conclusion that charging is harmless, superior or irrelevant for poorer noneligible populations.

test.mechanism_chain: Parental fee -> signal of investment/psychological ownership -> greater agency or sustained use
test.strongest_rival: Free ownership supports agency equally, or physical access dominates; higher fee-arm point estimates are sampling variation.
test.discriminating_observation: Test fee-versus-free contrasts directly and measure ownership/investment beliefs before outcomes.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S11 reports no precise between-arm differences on these outcomes; older abstract’s stronger fee narrative is not adopted.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Only one nominal fee and restricted setting; cannot rule out smaller effects, selective reporting or other fee sizes.

statement: In Zambia’s May2025 manuscript, the package improved selected self-reported agency measures, notably locus of control and bargaining, but general mobility and pooled aspirations were imprecise; aggregate empowerment varies with specification/correction. The final abstract says educational aspirations improved, an unresolved difference from the inspected pooled tables. The inspected evidence does not identify a distinct norm-change mechanism.

sources.supports: Main locus-control0.18SD/bargaining0.21SD; controlled appendix0.16/0.19 with corrected p-values .02/.04 and <=.01. Pooled aspirations0.07(SE0.05) in Table3 and0.06(SE0.05), corrected p=.44/.50 in TableA.11. Behavioural games discontinued.

States that educational aspirations improved; final tables/outcome definitions and pooled-versus-arm-specific interpretation not inspected. This records the version discrepancy, not corroboration of a positive pooled effect.

counterevidence: Aggregate index p-value .04 or .12 across adjustment families in manuscript appendix; no direct normative mediator randomised. Final abstract’s positive aspirations assertion is not reconciled with manuscript pooled estimates; no inference that final tables changed. Asset custody rules constrain movement and resale.
inference_limits: Causal identification is confined to the randomised package’s effects on the measured questionnaire indices in the inspected manuscript. Demand/salience versus deeper agency or norm change is not separated. These are neither unrestricted freedom nor adult earnings/occupation outcomes; final full-text reconciliation remains open.

test.mechanism_chain: Supported school transport -> changed daily constraints/experience -> selected reported agency dimensions
test.strongest_rival: Interview demand, asset salience or family reallocation changes reports without broad social norms changing.
test.discriminating_observation: Independent behavioural or longitudinal agency measures and a design separating response salience/demand from durable control; pre/post questionnaire measurement and multiple-testing corrections alone cannot discriminate this rival.
test.evidence_sought_found: PSY-S11 randomised survey-index contrasts and appendix corrections support some reported dimensions; they do not distinguish the stated response mechanism rival. Behavioural games were discontinued (§4.4.3) and supply no confirmation. S14 aspirations assertion remains unresolved against manuscript pooled tables.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Mechanism among saved time, safety, ownership, school exposure and survey response changes remains underdetermined; self-report not blind.

statement: After H4's sea trials, the Board commissioned Kendall to copy it; K1's 1769 completion and Cook-voyage operation provide a named replication by another maker, not evidence of economical serial manufacture.

sources.supports: 1766 commission, 1769 completion and second Cook voyage use.
Contemporary account presents the commission as a test of another maker's execution.

counterevidence: The obituary's approximate delivery date differs; RMG's completion date is used, with the disagreement preserved.
inference_limits: One copy establishes neither typical manufacturing yield nor fleet-wide access.

test.reason: Identifies a particular copy and trial, without assigning a causal effect to commission funding.

statement: Kendall's obituary reports cleaning K1 in 1775 and, after deterioration and stoppage on Cook's third voyage, replacing some corroded parts; a working precision artifact therefore did not remove the need for service during its useful life.

sources.supports: Reports disassembly/cleaning, altered rate, stoppage and rust requiring new parts.

counterevidence: The account is laudatory and cannot establish whether contamination, handling, design or another cause produced the failure.
inference_limits: No breakdown probability or comparative maintenance cost is inferred.

test.mechanism_chain: Long voyage exposure/operation -> rate change and deterioration -> service and part replacement -> repair work on a still-valued instrument.
test.strongest_rival: Exceptional mistreatment, not an inherent design burden, may explain this breakdown.
test.discriminating_observation: Comparable watches with documented handling/cleaning and rate histories would separate design vulnerability from an exceptional service episode.
test.evidence_sought_found: S02 explicitly records both successful voyages and later corrosion; no matched watch/handling records inspected.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Shows actual maintenance work, but not why that amount was needed or how representative it was.

statement: In the late eighteenth-century navigation system described by Higgitt, marine timekeepers and astronomical observations were used together; chronometer deployment did not make local-time observation or independent checks dispensable.

sources.locator: Investing in longitude and Navigation systems, notes 24 and 28–33
sources.supports: Joint trials, local time comparison, calibration and continued astronomical practice.

counterevidence: Relative reliance on methods differed by voyage and task; ordinary dead reckoning persisted.
inference_limits: No claim that every navigator made every observation or that one method was always best.

test.mechanism_chain: Portable reference time + observed local time/rate checks -> usable longitude comparison -> complementary instrument/observer work.
test.strongest_rival: A simple replacement account predicts astronomy becomes unnecessary when a good watch arrives.
test.discriminating_observation: Named joint use and the need to identify/restore a disturbed reference would contradict complete replacement.
test.evidence_sought_found: S03 describes combined Cook trials, calibration and local-time measurements; mathematical comparison also requires both reference and local information.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Chronometer convenience may reduce some lunar work; complementarity does not imply equal effort or unchanged practice.

statement: Japanese clockmakers served seasonal-hour conventions through different mechanisms, including alternating foliots and movable hour markers; many required periodic human adjustment rather than adoption of equal-hour time.

sources.supports: Explains alternating foliots, marker adjustment and two automatic exceptions.
Defines seasonal-hour system and recurring adjustment.

counterevidence: Surviving examples overrepresent durable/collectable artifacts; local calendars and practice were not necessarily uniform.
inference_limits: Technical alternatives do not establish nationwide household ownership or punctuality.

test.reason: Describes documented mechanism configurations and operator tasks, not the cause or prevalence of their adoption.

statement: Tanaka's 1851 Myriad Year Clock automated seasonal markers, yet Hashimoto reports only one completed clock and no buyer despite an intention to sell more; exceptional mechanical elaboration did not itself establish a scalable product.

sources.supports: Disassembly account, complex mechanism and unsold single-clock history; price-refusal story is explicitly anecdotal.

counterevidence: Tanaka subsequently changed work under patronage; opportunity costs and lack of marketing may rival price/complexity. The purchaser story is not an account ledger.
inference_limits: No calculated profitability, buyer willingness-to-pay or typical Japanese manufacturing limit.

test.mechanism_chain: Elaborate automatically adjusting design -> costly/complex individual artifact -> intended elite sale fails -> no observed repeated production.
test.strongest_rival: A career change or limited sales opportunity, rather than excessive complexity, explains the singular output.
test.discriminating_observation: Workshop accounts, offers, orders and later reproduction attempts could distinguish price/production constraints from changed priorities.
test.evidence_sought_found: S04 supplies artifact study and biographical sales narrative, but not accounts or a reproducibility trial by another maker.
test.remaining_ambiguity: Single output is better established than its cause; complexity is not treated as a sufficient explanation.

statement: Tanaka's documented career combined commercial craft work, instruction in calendrical theory/practice from the Tsuchimikado family in 1847, and later Saga patronage; the exact tools used to make his clock's fine components remain uncertain.

sources.supports: Shop/patronage sequence, specialist instruction and explicit uncertainty about clockmaking tools.

counterevidence: Career reconstruction relies partly on biographies and selected surviving records; some youthful-inventor anecdotes are unreliable.
inference_limits: This is a named route to expertise, not proof of the necessary educational sequence or relative contributions of teaching and self-practice.
